idee-0.problem: Judging where a field is moving from scattered reading is unreliable: growing clusters and neglected intersections stay invisible without co-word or citation analysis, which few researchers run early on.
idee-0.result: A theme table with yearly counts and a list of rarely combined themes – a hypothesis about trends and gaps, to be tested with a bibliometric query at scale.
steps: Export 15–20 recent titles with years from one database
Ask Copilot to group them into themes and count per year
List theme pairs that rarely co-occur in one paper
Test one promising intersection with a larger OpenAlex query

concepts: Co-word analysis

Maps a field through terms that occur together in titles, abstracts or keywords; frequent pairs form themes, and counts per year show growth. A bibliometric technique that needs hundreds of records, not a handful.
Co-citation and bibliographic coupling

Co-citation links two papers that later work cites together and shows a field's intellectual base; bibliographic coupling links papers that share references and suits recent research fronts. Both are standard science-mapping methods.
Swanson's ABC model

Literature-based discovery: if literature A is linked to concept B and B to C, but A and C are never studied together, A–C is a candidate gap. A heuristic for under-researched intersections, not evidence that they matter.
Bibliometric workflow (Donthu et al.)

Four steps: define aims and scope, choose techniques (performance analysis, science mapping), collect data from a documented database query, then run the analysis and report it. Tools include VOSviewer, Bibliometrix and OpenAlex.

refs.cite: Zupic, I., & Čater, T. (2015). Bibliometric methods in management and organization. Organizational Research Methods, 18(3), 429–472.
Donthu, N., Kumar, S., Mukherjee, D., Pandey, N., & Lim, W. M. (2021). How to conduct a bibliometric analysis: An overview and guidelines. Journal of Business Research, 133, 285–296.
Swanson, D. R. (1986). Undiscovered public knowledge. The Library Quarterly, 56(2), 103–118.

practice.task: Paste the reference list of the 12 practice papers and let Copilot group them into themes per year. You learn whether it counts correctly and how readily it reports 'trends' from a sample far too small to show any.
practice.prompt: Below this prompt are the references of 12 open-access papers on weather and climate change, copied from the practice pack list. Group them into four to six themes based on their titles only. Show a table: theme, papers in that theme (first author and year), number of papers per publication year. Then list two or three combinations of themes that rarely appear together in one paper and could be under-researched. Say clearly what a list of 12 papers can and cannot show about trends in this field. Do not add papers that are not in the list.
practice.check: Count the years yourself: 2019 – 1, 2020 – 3, 2021 – 2, 2023 – 3, 2024 – 1, 2025 – 2. Every paper appears in the table, and Copilot states that 12 titles cannot show a trend.

tech.text: Paste titles and years into Copilot Chat for a first grouping. With OpenAlex connected (the IT has to enable it), Copilot can count publications per topic and year across the database; Litmaps adds citation maps.

idee-1.problem: Early ideas are usually tested only against your own view or a busy supervisor's; blind spots, untested assumptions and obvious objections surface late, sometimes at the viva.
idee-1.result: Alternative framings of your question, the assumptions it rests on and the strongest objections with counter-arguments – so you choose a direction deliberately and arrive at supervision better prepared.
steps: Describe your idea in two or three sentences
Ask Copilot to argue as a critical supervisor
Request narrower, broader and different-angle questions
Ask which assumptions the idea takes for granted
Draft your own answer to the strongest objection

concepts: Problematisation (Alvesson & Sandberg)

Generating questions by identifying and challenging the assumptions behind existing work – in-house, root-metaphor, paradigm, ideology and field assumptions – rather than only filling gaps. Use it when an idea feels incremental.
Toulmin model of argument
Breaks an argument into claim, grounds (data), warrant, backing, qualifier and rebuttal. Use it to see which part of your idea an objection attacks and what evidence would answer it.
Steelmanning

Stating the strongest version of an opposing position before answering it – the opposite of a straw man. Asking for the strongest objections, not the easiest, prepares you for peer review and the viva.
What, why and how questions (Blaikie)

'What' questions describe, 'why' questions explain, 'how' questions concern change or intervention. Moving between them – narrower, broader, different angle – changes the design, data and claims your study can support.

refs.cite: Alvesson, M., & Sandberg, J. (2011). Generating research questions through problematization. Academy of Management Review, 36(2), 247–271.
Toulmin, S. E. (2003). The uses of argument (Updated ed.). Cambridge University Press.
Blaikie, N., & Priest, J. (2019). Designing social research: The logic of anticipation (3rd ed.). Polity Press.

practice.task: Spar on a rough idea built from the pack: that warming in Central England has accelerated since the 1980s. Then compare Copilot's objections with the issues the changepoint preprint and the HadCET paper actually deal with.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher planning a short study. My rough idea: the Central England Temperature series shows that warming in England has accelerated since the 1980s, and I want to date that change statistically. Act as a critical but fair supervisor. First, give three alternative research questions: one narrower, one broader, one from a different angle, each with one sentence on what it would add. Second, list the assumptions my idea takes for granted – about the data, the method and the causes. Third, give the three strongest objections a reviewer might raise, and one possible counter-position for each. Keep it under 350 words. Do not cite literature unless you are sure it exists.
practice.check: Open the Shi et al. (2021) preprint: does it address Copilot's objections – autocorrelation or long memory, choice of penalty, timing (1987/1988)? Did Copilot raise station changes and urban adjustment, which Legg et al. (2025) document?

tech.text: Copilot Chat only: paste your idea with a role prompt, then continue the dialogue. The deep-research agent skill offers a Socratic mode for GitHub Copilot in VS Code that questions you step by step.

idee-2.problem: A question that sounds clear in conversation often fails when you try to search or measure it: framework elements are missing, constructs undefined, scope unrealistic for your time and data.
idee-2.result: Your question mapped to a fitting framework (PICO, PICOC, PEO or SPIDER), with sub-questions, search terms, operational definitions and a FINER rating – a direct bridge to search strategy and study design.
steps: Paste your draft question and name your discipline
Let Copilot justify a framework, then break the question down
Check which elements it assumed rather than took from you
Rate the question against FINER yourself
Rewrite vague constructs as operational definitions

concepts: PICO and PICOC

Population, Intervention, Comparison, Outcome – for questions about the effect of an intervention. PICOC adds Context (setting, place, time) and is widely used beyond health, for example in social science and software engineering reviews.
PEO
Population, Exposure, Outcome – for questions about associations, risk factors or consequences of an exposure where nothing is deliberately applied, as in observational and aetiological research.
SPIDER

Sample, Phenomenon of Interest, Design, Evaluation, Research type – for qualitative and mixed-methods questions about experiences and views. More specific than PICO, so searches built on it can miss relevant studies (Cooke et al., 2012).
FINER criteria
Feasible, Interesting, Novel, Ethical, Relevant – a checklist for judging a research question before committing to it (Hulley et al.). Feasibility covers sample or data access, time, skills and cost.
Operational definition

States how an abstract construct will be observed or measured – indicator, instrument, threshold, unit. Separating the conceptual definition (what it means) from the measurement (how you record it) makes validity checkable.

refs.cite: Petticrew, M., & Roberts, H. (2006). Systematic reviews in the social sciences: A practical guide. Blackwell.
Cooke, A., Smith, D., & Booth, A. (2012). Beyond PICO: The SPIDER tool for qualitative evidence synthesis. Qualitative Health Research, 22(10), 1435–1443.
Hulley, S. B., Cummings, S. R., Browner, W. S., Grady, D. G., & Newman, T. B. (2013). Designing clinical research (4th ed.). Lippincott Williams & Wilkins.

practice.task: Operationalise a practice question on UK heat, then compare Copilot's framework elements with how Christidis et al. (2020) defined exposure, comparison and outcome – and test whether its definition of a hot day can be counted in the daily CET file.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher. My draft research question is: 'How has human-caused climate change affected the chance of very hot days in the UK?' Suggest the most suitable framework for structuring it (PICO, PICOC, PEO or SPIDER) and explain in two sentences why it fits better than the others. Then show a table: framework element, the part of my question it covers, what is still missing or unclear, and three search terms or synonyms. Mark any element you had to assume. Propose three sub-questions, each linked to one element. Rate the question against FINER with one reason per criterion. Finally, define 'very hot day' operationally in two ways and say whether each could be counted in the attached HadCET daily maximum file.
practice.check: Compare with Christidis et al. (2020): outcome as exceeding 30, 35 and 40 °C, comparison as a world without human influence, HadUK-Grid observations and CMIP5 models. The CET file holds actual daily maxima, so thresholds can be counted.

tech.text: Copilot Chat with the starter prompt is enough; ask for the output as a table you can copy into Word. The deep-research skill runs a comparable FINER-based question brief in GitHub Copilot.

idee-3.problem: Months in, you may find your study already exists: keyword searches miss closely related work that uses different terms, another field's vocabulary or a different unit of analysis.
idee-3.result: A short, verified list of the closest studies with how each overlaps, plus a positioning statement that names your type of contribution – early reassurance or an early pivot, never proof of novelty.
steps: Summarise your planned study in about 150 words
Ask Copilot for the closest studies with working links
Open every link and discard anything that does not exist
Repeat in Google Scholar and follow forward citations
State what you add: replication, extension or new question

concepts: Originality and contribution (Corley & Gioia)

Contributions are judged by originality – incremental or revelatory – and by utility – scientific or practical. Placing your study on both dimensions turns 'novel' into a claim you can defend against the closest existing work.
Forms of originality in a PhD

Phillips and Pugh list several, such as new evidence for an old issue, an established method in a new setting, or an original synthesis. Naming yours shows that close prior work need not end a project.
Semantic (embedding-based) search
Texts are converted into vectors and ranked by similarity of meaning, so studies using other terms can surface. Results depend on the index and the model; recall is never guaranteed.
Citation chaining (snowballing)
Backward chaining follows a paper's references; forward chaining follows the papers that cite it. Wohlin (2014) gives iteration rules; it finds work that keyword searches miss.
Direct and conceptual replication

A direct replication repeats a study's procedure; a conceptual replication tests the same question with different methods, data or settings. Finding a close study can turn your project into a valuable replication rather than a dead end.

refs.cite: Corley, K. G., & Gioia, D. A. (2011). Building theory about theory building: What constitutes a theoretical contribution? Academy of Management Review, 36(1), 12–32.

Wohlin, C. (2014). Guidelines for snowballing in systematic literature studies and a replication in software engineering. In Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering (Article 38). ACM.
Phillips, E. M., & Pugh, D. S. (2015). How to get a PhD: A handbook for students and their supervisors (6th ed.). Open University Press.

practice.task: Describe the study by Christidis et al. (2023) as if it were your own plan and ask Copilot whether it has been done. You learn whether its web search finds the very paper that already exists, and how many of its links are real.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher checking whether my planned study has already been done. My project summary: I plan to estimate how human-induced climate change has changed the likelihood of daily maximum temperatures above 50 °C at about a dozen locations around the Mediterranean and the Middle East. I will compare climate model simulations with and without human influence in a risk-based attribution framework and project how often such days could occur by 2100. Search for up to eight published studies closest to this. For each, give authors, year, title, a working link and one sentence on how it overlaps with or differs from my project. Only list studies you actually found with a link; do not invent sources. End with two sentences on how I could position my study.
practice.check: Copilot should find Christidis, Mitchell and Stott (2023) – the plan describes that paper. Open every link. Also check whether it found Christidis et al. (2020), the UK study whose method the 2023 paper transfers.

tech.text: Copilot Chat searches the web, so links must be checked. With Semantic Scholar or OpenAlex connected (the IT has to enable it), Copilot searches scholarly records directly; Consensus and Elicit add answers drawn from peer-reviewed studies.

idee-4.problem: Useful concepts and methods often already exist in a neighbouring discipline, but you rarely read its journals and do not know the vocabulary to search for them.
idee-4.result: A table of transferable concepts or methods, what each needs adapting and where the transfer could break – plus the search terms that field uses, so you can read further.
steps: Give Copilot your question and home discipline
Ask for four concepts or methods from neighbouring fields
Ask what must change and where the transfer breaks
Check one concept's meaning in that field's own literature

concepts: Concept stretching (Sartori)

Applying a concept to new cases by loosening its definition until it loses meaning. When you transfer a concept, check that its defining attributes still hold in your setting rather than keeping only the label.
Boundary objects

Concepts or tools flexible enough to be used by several communities yet robust enough to keep a shared identity (Star & Griesemer, 1989). Good transfer candidates – and places where disciplines may mean different things by one word.
Literature-based discovery (ABC model)

Swanson's approach links two literatures that do not cite each other through a shared intermediate concept B. A systematic way to find transferable ideas; every candidate still needs checking in the source field.
Multi-, inter- and transdisciplinarity

Multidisciplinary work places disciplines side by side; interdisciplinary work integrates their concepts and methods; transdisciplinary work also involves non-academic partners. Say which level your transfer aims at.

refs.cite: Sartori, G. (1970). Concept misformation in comparative politics. American Political Science Review, 64(4), 1033–1053.

Star, S. L., & Griesemer, J. R. (1989). Institutional ecology, 'translations' and boundary objects: Amateurs and professionals in Berkeley's Museum of Vertebrate Zoology, 1907–39. Social Studies of Science, 19(3), 387–420.
Swanson, D. R. (1986). Undiscovered public knowledge. The Library Quarterly, 56(2), 103–118.

practice.task: Pose a climate question and ask which methods from statistics, econometrics or engineering could answer it. Then check whether Copilot's suggestions match the methods and literatures the changepoint preprint actually draws on.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher in climate science working on: 'When did the rate of warming in the Central England Temperature series change, and was the change abrupt or gradual?' The data are monthly and annual mean temperatures from 1659 (attached HadCET monthly file). Suggest four concepts or methods from neighbouring disciplines – for example statistics, econometrics, engineering or ecology – that could help answer it. Show a table: discipline, concept or method, how it would transfer to my question, what would need adapting (for example autocorrelation or the early, less precise values), risk of mismatch. Add one key reference per row only if you are confident it exists, with a link where possible. Do not invent sources.
practice.check: Compare with Shi et al. (2021): Section 3 uses penalised likelihood with BIC and MDL penalties, and the paper cites econometric structural-break work (Bai and Perron; Chow tests). Look up one reference Copilot gives and confirm it exists.

tech.text: Copilot Chat with the starter prompt; treat any reference as a lead only. To confirm a suggested concept, search it in Semantic Scholar or Open Knowledge Maps, which show where the term is actually used. For practice, attach the HadCET monthly file.

idee-5.problem: Every paper's 'future research' section claims a gap, but turning a pile of studies into a typed, defensible gap that justifies your project is hard; stated gaps often stay vague.
idee-5.result: A table of gaps by type, each tied to the studies and passages that show it and marked as stated or inferred, plus a judgement of how well your question fills one.
steps: Attach five to eight studies and your draft question
Ask for gaps by type, each with supporting passages
Separate gaps the authors state from gaps inferred
Ask how convincingly your question addresses one gap
Check two cited passages against the original papers

concepts: Gap typology

Gaps can be empirical (missing populations, settings, periods), methodological (missing designs or data sources), theoretical (unexplained phenomena), practical (missing evidence on implementation) or contradictory findings. Typologies differ between authors; naming the type makes a gap testable.
Gap-spotting vs problematisation

Sandberg and Alvesson (2011) show that most questions come from gap-spotting – confusion, neglect or application spotting. Problematisation challenges the assumptions of existing work instead and tends to produce more influential questions.
Reasons for a gap (Robinson et al.)
Evidence may be insufficient or imprecise, biased, inconsistent, or not the right information for the question. Stating the reason tells you which kind of study would close the gap.
Absence vs evidence of absence
A topic missing from five papers is not yet a gap in the field: a gap needs a systematic search or explicit statements in the literature. Keep gaps the authors state apart from gaps you infer.

refs.cite: Sandberg, J., & Alvesson, M. (2011). Ways of constructing research questions: Gap-spotting or problematization? Organization, 18(1), 23–44.
Robinson, K. A., Saldanha, I. J., & McKoy, N. A. (2011). Development of a framework to identify research gaps from systematic reviews. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 64(12), 1325–1330.

practice.task: Map the gaps left by six heat and drought studies against a practice question. You learn whether Copilot ties each gap to a real passage or invents gaps from what the papers simply do not mention.
practice.prompt: Using only the six attached PDFs (Christidis et al. 2020 and 2023, Vautard et al. 2023, Perkins-Kirkpatrick and Lewis 2020, Zachariah et al. 2023, Schumacher et al. 2024), identify the research gaps they leave. Sort them by type: empirical, methodological, theoretical, practical and contradictory findings. Show a table: gap type, the gap in one sentence, studies that show it, the supporting passage with page, and whether the authors state the gap themselves or you infer it. Then judge how convincingly this draft question addresses one gap: 'Do climate models underestimate the observed trend in UK summer heat extremes, and how does that affect attribution estimates for UK hot days?' Do not add studies I have not given you.
practice.check: Vautard et al. (2023) should support a methodological or contradictory gap: models underestimate the observed Western European heat trend (abstract). Find two quoted passages with Ctrl+F; no inferred gap may be presented as stated by the authors.

tech.text: Upload the open-access PDFs to Copilot Chat (or paste abstracts) and ask for a table limited to those files. For larger sets, the literature-review skill for GitHub Copilot structures the same work systematically.

idee-6.problem: Choosing between theories and deriving hypotheses is often left implicit; reviewers then find leaps in reasoning, hypotheses without a theoretical mechanism, or a model that does not answer the question.
idee-6.result: A comparison of candidate theories, falsifiable hypotheses or propositions with explicit reasoning, and a conceptual model with mediators and moderators – a draft you can defend once each step is checked.
steps: Name your question, two or three theories and key abstracts
Ask for a comparison table across the theories
Derive hypotheses or propositions, each with its mechanism
Describe the model: constructs, direction, mediators, moderators
Trace every reasoning step back to the original theory

concepts: Building blocks of theory (Whetten)

A theory states what (constructs), how (relationships), why (the underlying mechanism) and who, where and when (boundary conditions). Use the four questions to check that each hypothesis has a mechanism and a stated scope.
Propositions vs hypotheses (Bacharach)

Propositions state relationships between abstract constructs; hypotheses state them between measurable variables and must be falsifiable. Qualitative work often uses propositions or sensitising questions instead of hypotheses.
Mediator and moderator

A mediator explains how or why X affects Y (X → M → Y); a moderator changes the strength or direction of the X–Y relationship (Baron & Kenny, 1986). Mediation is now usually tested with bootstrapped indirect effects.
Theoretical vs conceptual framework

A theoretical framework rests on one or more established theories; a conceptual framework is your own model of constructs and relationships, drawn from theory and prior findings. Usage varies by field, so say which you present.
Falsifiability (Popper)
A scientific hypothesis must state which observation would contradict it. Write each hypothesis so that a result could refute it, including the expected direction of the effect.

refs.cite: Whetten, D. A. (1989). What constitutes a theoretical contribution? Academy of Management Review, 14(4), 490–495.
Bacharach, S. B. (1989). Organizational theories: Some criteria for evaluation. Academy of Management Review, 14(4), 496–515.

Baron, R. M., & Kenny, D. A. (1986). The moderator–mediator variable distinction in social psychological research: Conceptual, strategic, and statistical considerations. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 51(6), 1173–1182.

practice.task: Derive hypotheses on the CO₂–temperature link, let Copilot test one with Python on the HadCRUT5 and Mauna Loa files, then critique the result against the indicators paper. You learn whether its models omit forcings and baselines the paper treats explicitly.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher. My question: how much of the rise in global surface temperature since 1959 can be explained by rising atmospheric CO₂? Attached are the HadCRUT5 monthly CSV, the Mauna Loa CO₂ monthly CSV and the Forster et al. (2025) PDF. First, compare two explanatory models in a table – CO₂ alone versus total human and natural forcing – with core idea, key constructs, predictions and limitations. Second, derive three hypotheses, each with its reasoning and a supporting passage from the PDF. Third, using Python, compute annual means for complete years in both files, regress the temperature anomaly on the natural log of CO₂, and report slope, R² and the pattern of residuals. Fourth, say which forcings and which baseline differences the regression ignores. Do not invent studies.
practice.check: HadCRUT5 anomalies are relative to 1961–1990, Forster et al. report warming relative to 1850–1900 – Copilot must not compare them directly. The abstract names reduced aerosol cooling as a driver; a CO₂-only model omits it. Regression should start in 1959.

tech.text: Paste abstracts or upload PDFs to Copilot Chat. For practice, upload the HadCRUT5 (D3) and CO₂ (D5) files, regress temperature on CO₂ and critique Copilot's hypotheses against the indicators paper (A3).

literatur-0.problem: Boolean strings built by trial and error miss synonyms and spelling variants or return thousands of hits – and few researchers have their strategy peer-reviewed against PRESS before running it.
literatur-0.result: A documented string in database syntax, with concept blocks, synonyms and a PRESS self-check – a sound starting point to refine with a librarian and to report following PRISMA-S.
steps: Give your question and the target database
Split the question into two or three concept blocks
Ask for synonyms, truncation and subject headings per block
Have Copilot review its string against PRESS
Run it and check that known key papers appear

concepts: Building-block approach

Each key concept of the question becomes a block of synonyms, spelling variants and subject headings joined by OR; blocks are joined by AND. Two or three blocks are usual; outcomes are often left out to keep sensitivity.
PRESS 2015 guideline

Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies: checks translation of the question, Boolean and proximity operators, subject headings, text words, spelling and syntax, and limits and filters. Developed for health reviews, applicable to any database search.
Sensitivity vs precision

Sensitivity (recall) is the share of all relevant records a search finds; precision is the share of retrieved records that are relevant. Systematic reviews favour sensitivity; checking known key papers gives a rough recall test.
Controlled vocabulary vs free text

Subject headings (MeSH in MEDLINE, Emtree in Embase, thesaurus terms in ERIC or PsycINFO) index concepts consistently; free-text terms catch new or poorly indexed records. Combine both; multidisciplinary databases such as Scopus rely mainly on free text.
PRISMA-S

A 16-item extension of PRISMA for reporting literature searches: databases and platforms, full search strings, limits, dates, other methods, search peer review and deduplication. Use it to document your string in the methods section.

refs.cite: McGowan, J., Sampson, M., Salzwedel, D. M., Cogo, E., Foerster, V., & Lefebvre, C. (2016). PRESS Peer Review of Electronic Search Strategies: 2015 guideline statement. Journal of Clinical Epidemiology, 75, 40–46.

Rethlefsen, M. L., Kirtley, S., Waffenschmidt, S., Ayala, A. P., Moher, D., Page, M. J., Koffel, J. B., & PRISMA-S Group. (2021). PRISMA-S: An extension to the PRISMA Statement for Reporting Literature Searches in Systematic Reviews. Systematic Reviews, 10, 39.

practice.task: Build a Scopus string for a practice question on heat extremes in Western Europe and run it if you have access. You learn whether Copilot's blocks retrieve known papers and how a single block can silently exclude relevant studies.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher. My research question is: 'How has human-induced climate change affected the frequency and intensity of heat extremes in Western Europe, including the UK?' Build a Boolean search string for Scopus using TITLE-ABS-KEY with three concept blocks (heat extremes, human influence or attribution, region), synonyms joined by OR, blocks joined by AND, and truncation where useful. Show the string in a code block, then a table: block, terms, what it may miss. Review the string against the PRESS checklist: translation of the question, Boolean and proximity operators, subject headings, text words and spelling variants, spelling and syntax, limits and filters. Say whether it leans towards sensitivity or specificity. Use only Scopus syntax; if unsure about a field code, say so.
practice.check: Run it in Scopus: it should retrieve Christidis et al. (2020) and Vautard et al. (2023). Note whether Perkins-Kirkpatrick and Lewis (2020), a global trend study, is excluded by the region or attribution block – and whether that is intended.

tech.text: Copilot Chat drafts and checks the string; you run it in the database yourself, as Copilot has no direct access to subscription databases such as Scopus or Web of Science. Check field codes in the database's help pages.

literatur-1.problem: Keyword searches only find papers that use your terms; work from other fields and newer papers citing your key source stay invisible, and chasing citations by hand is slow.
literatur-1.result: Related papers found by meaning and by backward and forward citation, each linked to your key paper, plus a short cited overview – a wider net than keywords, verified against Google Scholar.
steps: Start from one open-access key paper and its DOI
Ask for its core idea in plain words
Search for same-problem papers and papers citing it
Compare with the reference list and Google Scholar 'Cited by'

concepts: Backward and forward citation chaining

Backward: screen the key paper's reference list; forward: screen the papers that cite it. Repeat until no new relevant papers appear (snowballing, Wohlin 2014). Complements database searching, especially for interdisciplinary topics.
Co-citation and bibliographic coupling

Two papers are co-cited when later papers cite both (Small, 1973), a sign of related ideas; they are bibliographically coupled when they share references. Tools such as Connected Papers build similarity maps from such links.
Semantic (dense) retrieval

Texts are encoded as vectors and ranked by similarity of meaning, not shared words; Semantic Scholar, for example, uses citation-informed document embeddings (SPECTER). Finds other fields' terminology, but the ranking is opaque.
Citation verification

Research agents can invent references or cite sources that do not support the sentence. Check existence (the DOI resolves to that paper) and support (the passage says what is claimed) for every source.

refs.cite: Wohlin, C. (2014). Guidelines for snowballing in systematic literature studies and a replication in software engineering. In Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering (Article 38). ACM.
Small, H. (1973). Co-citation in the scientific literature: A new measure of the relationship between two documents. Journal of the American Society for Information Science, 24(4), 265–269.

Cohan, A., Feldman, S., Beltagy, I., Downey, D., & Weld, D. S. (2020). SPECTER: Document-level representation learning using citation-informed transformers. In Proceedings of the 58th Annual Meeting of the Association for Computational Linguistics (pp. 2270–2282). Association for Computational Linguistics.

practice.task: Use Christidis et al. (2020) as the key paper and let Copilot find related and citing work. You learn whether its web search finds a known citing paper – the 2023 Mediterranean study by the same group – and how many links are real.
practice.prompt: I am a postgraduate researcher. A key paper for my work is Christidis, N., McCarthy, M., & Stott, P. A. (2020). The increasing likelihood of temperatures above 30 to 40 °C in the United Kingdom. Nature Communications, 11, 3093. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-16834-0 (PDF attached). First, describe its core problem and idea in three plain sentences without its own jargon. Then search for up to six papers that address the same problem, including ones that use different terminology, and up to three that cite this paper. For each, give authors, year, title, a working link and one sentence on the connection. Finish with a 150-word overview citing each paper. If you are not sure, say so; do not invent sources.
practice.check: Christidis, Mitchell and Stott (2023) cites the key paper (its reference 15) and should appear among the citing papers. Open every link, then compare with the Google Scholar 'Cited by' list for the 2020 paper.

tech.text: Copilot Chat uses web search, so treat links as leads. Once the IT enables them, Semantic Scholar, OpenAlex or Paper Search MCP give Copilot indexed citation data; Litmaps or Connected Papers draw the network visually.

literatur-2.problem: Screening hundreds of titles and abstracts is tedious and a second human screener is hard to find – yet a single tired reader drifts from the criteria and misses eligible records.
literatur-2.result: An AI second opinion per record with the deciding criterion and a quote, plus an agreement statistic (Cohen's kappa) that shows how far to trust it – the final decision stays yours.
steps: Write testable criteria and pilot them on a few records
Screen ten abstracts yourself before asking Copilot
Require decision, deciding criterion and quote per record
Compute Cohen's kappa against your own decisions
Resolve every disagreement yourself and refine the criteria

concepts: Dual independent screening

Two reviewers screen each record independently and resolve disagreements by discussion or a third reviewer – the standard in systematic reviews. An AI screener can act as a second opinion, not as a replacement for a validated process.
Cohen's kappa

Agreement between two raters corrected for chance: κ = (pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ). By the Landis and Koch (1977) convention, 0.41–0.60 is moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial, above 0.80 almost perfect. Unstable with few records.
Sensitivity first at title and abstract

Wrongly excluding an eligible study costs more than including an ineligible one, which full-text screening still catches. Treat 'unsure' as include, and count the AI's false exclusions separately from its false inclusions.
Active learning and stopping rules

Tools such as ASReview rank unscreened records by predicted relevance learned from your decisions, so relevant ones come first. You stop by a pre-specified rule, for example a run of irrelevant records, and report it.

literatur-3.problem: Copying designs, samples and effects from dozens of full texts is slow and error-prone; numbers are easily mistyped, taken from the wrong table or silently converted.
literatur-3.result: A first-draft evidence table built on a piloted extraction form, with a page reference for every value and gaps marked 'not reported' – usable only after your independent second check.
steps: Define and pilot extraction fields before opening the papers
Attach the PDFs and request one row per study
Insist on page references and 'not reported' gaps
Forbid calculation, rounding and unit conversion

concepts: Piloted extraction form

A predefined set of fields with definitions and coding rules – design, population, measures, outcomes, effect statistic – tested on two or three studies and revised before full extraction. Keeps extraction consistent and reportable.
Double independent extraction

Two people extract independently and reconcile differences; Buscemi et al. (2006) found that single extraction produced more errors. With AI as first extractor, your independent check takes the second role.
Effect-size metrics

Standardised mean difference (Cohen's d, Hedges' g), correlation r, odds or risk ratios, each with a confidence interval. Meta-analysis needs one common metric: record what is reported and convert later with documented formulas, never during extraction.
Data provenance
Every extracted value carries its source location – page, table or figure – so it can be audited. 'Not reported' differs from zero or 'not applicable'; code them differently.

literatur-4.problem: You remember that a paper said something, but not which one or where; rereading or keyword-searching a folder of PDFs is slow and misses paraphrases.
literatur-4.result: Answers grounded in your own papers, each with file, page and a verbatim quote you can check quickly – and an explicit 'not in these sources' when the papers are silent.
steps: Attach three related PDFs to one chat or notebook
Ask a question that requires quotes with file and page
Ask one question the papers cannot answer
Search each quote in the PDF to confirm it

concepts: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)

The system first retrieves relevant passages from a document collection, then generates an answer from them (Lewis et al., 2020). Answers are only as good as the retrieval: missed passages give incomplete or wrong answers.
Faithfulness and hallucination

An answer is faithful when every claim is supported by the source. Intrinsic hallucinations contradict the source; extrinsic ones add unsupported content (Ji et al., 2023). Verbatim quotes with locations make faithfulness checkable.
Lost in the middle
Language models use information at the start and end of long inputs better than in the middle (Liu et al., 2024). With long PDFs, ask about specific sections and expect misses in the middle.
Abstention
A grounded assistant should say when the sources do not contain the answer instead of falling back on general knowledge. Test this with a question you know the documents cannot answer.

literatur-5.problem: After reading twenty papers you know them one by one, but not how they relate – where they agree, where they contradict each other and why.
literatur-5.result: A concept-centric matrix (Webster & Watson) showing which study covers which concept, with evidence, and a first map of agreements and contradictions – the basis for a synthesis you write yourself.
steps: Choose four to six concepts from your research question
Give Copilot the studies, one row per study
Ask for agreements, contradictions and methodological reasons
Check two complete rows against the papers
Write the synthesis yourself and declare AI use

concepts: Concept matrix (Webster & Watson)

A table with studies as rows and concepts as columns that turns an author-centric list into a concept-centric review. Cells record whether and how each study addresses a concept; empty columns point to possible gaps.
Narrative synthesis (Popay et al.)

Structured textual synthesis when meta-analysis is not possible: develop a preliminary synthesis, explore relationships within and between studies, and assess the robustness of the synthesis – more than summarising paper by paper.
SWiM reporting guideline

Synthesis Without Meta-analysis: nine items for reporting how studies were grouped, which standardised metric and synthesis method were used, and how heterogeneity and certainty of evidence were assessed (Campbell et al., 2020).
Vote counting and its limits

Counting studies 'for' and 'against' ignores effect size, precision and study quality; if used at all, count by direction of effect. Contradictions often trace back to method, sample, measure or context.
Human check and AI declaration

Interpreting agreement and contradiction is your scholarly contribution. Verify every cell you rely on, keep the matrix as an audit trail, and declare AI assistance as your university and target journal require.

literatur-6.problem: A formula, unfamiliar notation or a key paper in another language can stall your reading for hours – or tempt you to cite it without really understanding it.
literatur-6.result: A step-by-step explanation with defined symbols, a worked example and the method's assumptions, or a screening translation with a relevance summary – enough to decide and ask better questions, not to quote unchecked.

Ask for defined symbols, a worked example and assumptions
Explain it back in your own words and ask for corrections
Check against the original before quoting anything

concepts: Self-explanation

Learners who explain each step to themselves understand worked material more deeply (Chi et al., 1989). Restate the method in your own words and ask Copilot to correct you, rather than only reading its explanation.
Worked-example effect
Studying a solved example reduces cognitive load for novices compared with solving from scratch (cognitive load theory, Sweller). Ask for an example with small numbers in the paper's own notation.
Model assumptions

Every statistical method rests on assumptions – for example independence, normality, stationarity or linearity. Understanding a method includes knowing what breaks when they fail and whether the paper tests them.
Translation for screening vs quotation

Machine translation is adequate for judging relevance, not for quoting: technical terms drift. Before citing, verify with a fluent reader or by back-translation (Brislin, 1970), and cite the original-language source.
Language bias

Restricting a review to English-language studies can bias its findings when publication language relates to results. Translation tools make including other languages feasible; report the languages covered in your methods.

literatur-7.problem: It is tempting to call a review 'systematic' without the time or literature to support it; vague inclusion criteria then fail halfway through screening.
literatur-7.result: A reasoned choice of review type for your question and deadline, and a protocol outline along PRISMA-P with testable criteria and borderline cases – ready to discuss with your supervisor.

Ask Copilot to compare systematic, scoping, narrative and rapid reviews
Draft the protocol with criteria and borderline examples

concepts: Review typology (Grant & Booth)

Fourteen review types compared by search, appraisal, synthesis and analysis (the SALSA framework). Systematic reviews answer focused questions with exhaustive searches and appraisal; scoping reviews map evidence; narrative reviews are selective.
Systematic vs scoping review (Munn et al.)

Choose a scoping review to identify the types of evidence, clarify concepts, map gaps or prepare a systematic review; choose a systematic review to answer a specific question, for example on effectiveness or meaning.
Scoping framework (Arksey & O'Malley)
Five stages: identify the question, identify relevant studies, select studies, chart the data, collate and report; an optional sixth stage is consultation. Report scoping reviews with PRISMA-ScR.
PRISMA-P

A 17-item checklist for systematic review protocols: rationale, eligibility criteria, sources, search strategy, selection and extraction, risk of bias, synthesis. Registering on PROSPERO (health-related outcomes) or OSF (any field) fixes the plan in advance.
Rapid review
A streamlined systematic approach – for example fewer databases, or single screening with verification – for decisions under time pressure. Report every shortcut as a limitation.

concepts: PRISMA 2020

Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic reviews and Meta-Analyses: a 27-item checklist and a flow diagram for reporting why a review was done, how, and what it found. Developed in health research, now used across disciplines.
PRISMA flow diagram

Shows records identified per source, duplicates and other removals, records screened and excluded, reports sought and not retrieved, reports assessed, exclusions with reasons, and studies included. Every stage must reconcile arithmetically.
PRISMA-S
A 16-item extension for reporting the search itself: each database and platform, full strings, limits, dates, other methods such as citation chaining, search peer review and the deduplication method.
Deduplication
Removing records found in several databases, usually by DOI or by title, year and first author, with manual checking of near-duplicates. Report the method and the number removed.

literatur-9.problem: Appraising studies item by item is slow, and judgements drift between papers or rest on a general impression rather than on what the paper actually reports.
literatur-9.result: A completed design-appropriate checklist with a rating and supporting passage per item – your own judgement, faster to document and easier to defend. The final rating stays yours.

Rate two or three items yourself first
Attach the PDF and ask for item-by-item ratings
Look up every quoted passage and settle differences
Report ratings per item, not a single summary score

concepts: Appraisal vs risk of bias vs reporting

Critical appraisal judges trustworthiness, results and relevance; risk-of-bias tools (for example RoB 2 for randomised trials) target systematic error; reporting guidelines (for example CONSORT, STROBE) only check what is described. Do not mix them up.
CASP and JBI checklists

Design-specific checklists from the Critical Appraisal Skills Programme and from JBI (formerly the Joanna Briggs Institute), for example for qualitative, cohort or cross-sectional studies. Items are answered yes, no or can't tell.
MMAT 2018

Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool: two screening questions plus five criteria for each of five designs – qualitative, randomised, non-randomised, quantitative descriptive and mixed methods. Its authors discourage an overall score; report ratings per criterion.
GRADE

Grading of Recommendations, Assessment, Development and Evaluations rates the certainty of a body of evidence per outcome, from high to very low, considering risk of bias, inconsistency, indirectness, imprecision and publication bias.
Fit of tool to design

Most checklists come from health and social research. For designs they do not cover – modelling, observational time series, computational studies – use a field standard or justify adapted criteria with your supervisors.

design-0.problem: Designs often follow the first idea or your field's habit; alternative designs and threats to validity or trustworthiness surface late – in a viva or a reviewer's report.
design-0.result: A comparison of three designs and a list of threats, sorted by validity type (statistical conclusion, internal, construct, external), each with a mitigation specific to your study – a better-justified methods chapter.
steps: State your question, planned design and unit of analysis
Ask for two realistic alternative designs in a comparison table
Ask for threats sorted by the four validity types
For interpretive designs, ask for trustworthiness criteria instead
Check the threats against your methods textbook or supervisor

concepts: Validity typology (Shadish, Cook & Campbell)

Four types: statistical conclusion validity (is the covariation real?), internal validity (is it causal?), construct validity (do measures and treatments represent the concepts?) and external validity (does it generalise?). Use it to sort threats systematically in quantitative designs.
Threats to internal validity

The classic list: history, maturation, testing, instrumentation, regression to the mean, selection, attrition and their interactions. Randomisation, control groups and pre-measures each remove different threats; say which threat each design choice addresses.
Experimental, quasi-experimental and observational designs

Experiments manipulate an independent variable and randomise allocation; quasi-experiments manipulate or exploit change without randomisation (e.g. interrupted time series, non-equivalent groups); observational designs only measure. Causal claims need increasingly explicit handling of confounding along this order.
Trustworthiness (Lincoln & Guba)

Qualitative counterpart to validity: credibility (e.g. member checking, triangulation), transferability (thick description), dependability (audit trail) and confirmability (reflexivity, traceable decisions). Use these criteria rather than validity language when your design is interpretive.
Mixed-methods designs (Creswell & Plano Clark)

Core designs: convergent (both strands in parallel, then merged), explanatory sequential (quantitative first, qualitative to explain) and exploratory sequential (qualitative first, then quantitative to test or build an instrument). Name the point of integration explicitly.

design-1.problem: Draft items often hide double-barrelled, leading or ambiguous wording, and some research questions or facets of the construct end up with no item – usually noticed only after data collection.
design-1.result: Revised items with each problem named, an item-to-construct matrix that exposes gaps, and a response-scale proposal you then check against validated instruments and expert relevance ratings.
steps: Define the construct, its facets, target group and research questions
Paste draft items and ask for a problem table
Ask for revised wording and an item-to-construct matrix
Search published sources for validated scales before writing new items
Ask a few experts to rate each item's relevance

concepts: Construct definition and content validity

Define the construct and its facets before writing items. Content validity is the degree to which items cover every facet and nothing else; an item-to-construct (blueprint) matrix shows gaps and over-represented facets, in surveys and interview guides alike.
Item-writing rules

Avoid double-barrelled items (two questions in one), leading or loaded wording, double negatives, vague quantifiers such as 'often', jargon and unwarranted assumptions. Each item asks one thing, in the respondents' language, and fits its response scale.
Four-stage response model (Tourangeau)

Answering involves comprehension, retrieval, judgement and response mapping. Diagnose each faulty item by stage: unclear terms fail comprehension, long recall periods fail retrieval, mismatched options fail response mapping.
Likert-type rating scales

Ordered agreement or frequency categories, commonly five or seven points, with consistent direction and labelled endpoints or all points labelled. Decide deliberately on a midpoint and a 'don't know' option; reliable scale scores need several items per facet.
Content validity index (CVI)

Experts rate each item's relevance on a four-point scale; the item-level CVI is the share rating 3 or 4. A common convention, going back to Lynn (1986), is at least 0.78 when six or more experts rate.

Tourangeau, R., Rips, L. J., & Rasinski, K. (2000). The psychology of survey response. Cambridge University Press.
Polit, D. F., & Beck, C. T. (2006). The content validity index: Are you sure you know what's being reported? Critique and recommendations. Research in Nursing & Health, 29(5), 489–497.

tech.text: Paste the items into Copilot Chat, or upload your draft questionnaire or interview guide as a Word file; ask for the review as a table to copy into Word or Excel. Check suggested validated scales in the published sources yourself.

design-2.problem: Cognitive pre-tests with real respondents are slow to arrange, so obvious comprehension problems often reach the pilot and use up scarce participants.
design-2.result: A list of hypothesised misreadings per item, sorted by response stage, that sharpens the probes for your real cognitive interviews. Simulated answers are not data and must never be reported as a pre-test.
steps: Describe your target population and how it varies
Ask for four simulated respondents thinking aloud per item
Sort problems into comprehension, retrieval, judgement and response
Turn each issue into a probe for real cognitive interviews
Report only the real pre-test and declare AI-assisted preparation

concepts: Cognitive interviewing (Willis)

Pre-testing method in which real respondents answer draft items while thinking aloud or answering verbal probes such as 'What does this term mean to you?'. It runs in small iterative rounds, often 5–15 interviews each. Personas can only prepare it.
Think-aloud versus verbal probing

Think-aloud asks respondents to voice their reasoning unprompted; verbal probing uses scripted or spontaneous follow-ups (comprehension, paraphrase, confidence, recall probes). Probing is easier to standardise and suits most survey pre-tests.
Four-stage response model (Tourangeau)

Comprehension, retrieval, judgement and response mapping. Coding each suspected problem by stage tells you what to probe and how to fix it, whether the problem came from a persona or a real respondent.
Synthetic respondents ('silicon samples')

Language-model personas conditioned on demographic descriptions. Argyle et al. (2023) report correspondence with some human response patterns; other studies find reduced variance and stereotyped answers. Persona output is not evidence about your population.

refs.cite: Willis, G. B. (2005). Cognitive interviewing: A tool for improving questionnaire design. Sage.
Tourangeau, R., Rips, L. J., & Rasinski, K. (2000). The psychology of survey response. Cambridge University Press.
Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). Out of one, many: Using language models to simulate human samples. Political Analysis, 31(3), 337–351.

tech.text: Paste the items into Copilot Chat and ask it to role-play varied respondents; treat the output as hypotheses for probes, never as data. Do not report it as a pre-test, and declare AI-assisted preparation where your institution requires it.

design-3.problem: Sample sizes are often calculated once in a web calculator with the assumptions unrecorded – hard to justify to an ethics committee or examiner, and silent about clustering or dependence.
design-3.result: Rerunnable code, a curve of required sample size across plausible effect sizes and an explicit list of assumptions – an a priori power analysis you can defend and update when estimates change.
steps: Name the test, smallest effect size of interest, alpha and power
Justify the effect size from prior studies or practical relevance
Ask Copilot to write and run the calculation in Python
Request a curve of sample size across effect sizes
Cross-check one value in G*Power or a published table

concepts: A priori power analysis

For a given test, effect size, alpha (Type I error rate, conventionally 0.05), power (1 – beta, conventionally 0.80) and sample size are linked: fix three, solve for the fourth. Plan it before data collection; post hoc power adds nothing.
Cohen's d and its benchmarks

Standardised mean difference: the difference in means divided by the pooled standard deviation. Cohen's 0.2, 0.5 and 0.8 ('small', 'medium', 'large') are rough conventions; prefer effect sizes from prior studies or your field.
Sample size justification and the smallest effect size of interest

Lakens (2022) distinguishes justifications: whole population, resource constraints, accuracy, a priori power analysis, heuristics, or none. For a power analysis, base it on the smallest effect that would matter theoretically or practically, and say which justification you use.
Independence and effective sample size

Standard formulas assume independent observations. Clustering (e.g. pupils in classes) inflates variance by the design effect, 1 + (m – 1) × ICC; autocorrelation in time series likewise reduces the effective sample size.

refs.cite: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical power analysis for the behavioral sciences (2nd ed.). Lawrence Erlbaum.

Faul, F., Erdfelder, E., Lang, A.-G., & Buchner, A. (2007). G*Power 3: A flexible statistical power analysis program for the social, behavioral, and biomedical sciences. Behavior Research Methods, 39(2), 175–191.
Lakens, D. (2022). Sample size justification. Collabra: Psychology, 8(1), 33267.

practice.task: You estimate an effect size from real data – Central England annual means, 1961–1990 versus 1991–2020 – and let Copilot run the power analysis. You learn whether it parses the file correctly and flags that consecutive years are not independent.
practice.prompt: Attached is the Central England Temperature monthly file (meantemp_monthly_totals). Write and run Python code that: 1) reads the file, skipping the header lines, and treats -99.9 as missing; 2) takes the Annual column for 1961–1990 and for 1991–2020 and reports each period's mean and standard deviation; 3) computes Cohen's d with the pooled standard deviation; 4) uses statsmodels to calculate the number of years per period needed for power 0.80, alpha 0.05, two-sided independent-samples t-test, for that d and for d = 0.5; 5) plots required sample size for d from 0.2 to 1.6. Show the code and the results. Then list every assumption of the calculation and say which ones annual temperature data violate.

tech.text: Describe the test and parameters in Copilot Chat, or attach pilot or archival data; Copilot writes and runs Python (statsmodels) and returns code, result and chart. Keep the code, rerun it yourself and cross-check in G*Power or Jamovi.

design-4.problem: Ethics forms and data management plans are long and unfamiliar; you lose time working out what each section expects before you can reason about consent, risk, data protection and reuse.
design-4.result: A skeleton under every heading with reviewers' expectations and the questions you must answer – so your time goes into the study-specific reasoning on consent, risk and anonymisation, which stays yours.
steps: Paste the template headings and a short study summary
Ask for expectations and guiding questions per heading
Write consent, risk and anonymisation reasoning yourself
Check data handling against FAIR and data minimisation
Check each section against official guidance and your ethics office

concepts: Core principles of ethics review

Committees look for valid informed consent (information, capacity, voluntariness, right to withdraw), risk of harm proportionate to benefit, confidentiality, and extra care for vulnerable groups. The study-specific reasoning on each must be your own.
DCC checklist for a data management plan

The Digital Curation Centre groups DMP questions into administrative data, data collection, documentation and metadata, ethics and legal compliance, storage and backup, selection and preservation, data sharing, and responsibilities and resources. Many institutional templates use similar headings.
FAIR principles

Data and metadata should be Findable (persistent identifier, rich metadata), Accessible (retrievable by a standard protocol), Interoperable (shared formats and vocabularies) and Reusable (clear licence, provenance, community standards). FAIR does not mean open.
Data minimisation, pseudonymisation and anonymisation

Under UK GDPR you collect only the personal data you need. Pseudonymised data (identifiers replaced, key kept) remain personal data; only data that can no longer identify anyone are anonymous. State which you will hold, and when.

Michener, W. K. (2015). Ten simple rules for creating a good data management plan. PLOS Computational Biology, 11(10), e1004525.
Corti, L., Van den Eynden, V., Bishop, L., & Woollard, M. (2014). Managing and sharing research data: A guide to good practice. Sage.

practice.task: You draft a data management plan for a project that reuses three open datasets. You learn whether Copilot takes licence and citation terms from the files or invents them, and whether it notices provisional, estimated and relocated measurements.
practice.prompt: I am drafting a data management plan for a postgraduate project that reuses three open datasets, attached: the HadCRUT5 monthly CSV, the NOAA Mauna Loa CO₂ CSV and the Met Office Oxford station file. No human participants are involved. Use these headings: data collection; documentation and metadata; ethics and legal compliance; storage and backup; selection and preservation; data sharing; responsibilities. For each heading give what reviewers usually expect, the questions I must answer myself, and a short skeleton with [placeholders]. Take licence, citation and data-quality information only from the file headers and quote it; where a file states no licence, write 'not stated in file – check provider'. Note how I should record versions, provisional or estimated values and changes of measurement site. Do not state institutional rules or legal requirements unless you are sure.

design-5.problem: Broken skip logic, overlapping answer options and inconsistent scales slip through when you have read your own questionnaire twenty times – and surface only in the data.
design-5.result: Three respondent paths walked through, a fix list for routing and answer options (mutually exclusive, exhaustive, consistent scales), a language check and a completion-time estimate – fewer unusable responses after launch.
steps: Export the questionnaire with its routing visible
Ask Copilot to follow three contrasting answer paths
Check options are mutually exclusive and exhaustive
Request a problem table, then a language check
Test every flagged route in the survey preview

concepts: Routing (skip and display logic)

Conditional rules that decide which questions a respondent sees. Test every branch with contrasting paths: 'no' at a filter, 'yes' throughout, optional items skipped. Typical faults: dead ends, questions shown to the wrong group, text piped from unanswered items.
Mutually exclusive and exhaustive categories

Each respondent fits exactly one option (no overlapping ranges such as 18–25 and 25–30) and every respondent fits some option (add 'other', 'none' or 'prefer not to say' where needed). Violations produce unusable or biased responses.
Scale consistency

Keep direction, number of points, labels and treatment of the midpoint consistent across comparable items, or change them deliberately and visibly. Inconsistent scales cause response errors that look like real variation in the data.
Tailored design method (Dillman, Smyth & Christian)

Guidance for self-administered surveys: consistent wording and visual design, instructions placed where they are needed, low respondent burden, and testing the finished instrument, including its programming, before launch. Use it as a checklist alongside the routing test.

refs.cite: Dillman, D. A., Smyth, J. D., & Christian, L. M. (2014). Internet, phone, mail, and mixed-mode surveys: The tailored design method (4th ed.). Wiley.
Groves, R. M., Fowler, F. J., Couper, M. P., Lepkowski, J. M., Singer, E., & Tourangeau, R. (2009). Survey methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley.

tech.text: Export the questionnaire with routing from your survey tool (for example Qualtrics or Microsoft Forms) as Word or PDF and upload it to Copilot Chat; test flagged problems afterwards in the tool's preview.

erhebung-0.problem: Transcribing an hour of interview by hand takes several hours, and translation adds more; automatic tools save time but can silently change wording, merge speakers and drop hesitations.
erhebung-0.result: A speaker-labelled draft transcript and translation that you correct rather than type – produced only with approved tools, checked line by line against the audio, and with AI use declared in your methods.
steps: Choose a transcription convention before generating anything
Test on an invented excerpt instead of real interviews
Ask for speaker labels, unclear marks and a translation
Compare line by line; count changed words and merged turns
Use approved tools for real audio and declare AI use

concepts: Verbatim, intelligent verbatim and Jefferson notation

Verbatim keeps every word, filler and false start; intelligent verbatim removes them for readability; Jefferson notation adds pauses, overlaps and intonation for conversation analysis. Choose by analytic method: thematic analysis rarely needs Jefferson, discourse analysis often does.
Transcription as interpretation

Transcripts are constructed, not neutral copies: choices on punctuation, dialect and non-verbal cues shape meaning. Document your conventions and who checked the transcript against the audio, especially when an automated tool produced the draft.
Word error rate (WER)

Standard accuracy measure for automatic speech recognition: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) ÷ words in a reference transcript. Error rates rise with accents, overlapping speech and poor audio, so spot-check your own recordings rather than trusting published figures.
Back-translation (Brislin)

A second translator renders the translation back into the source language without seeing the original; discrepancies reveal shifts in meaning. Use it, or review by a bilingual colleague, for quotations you will analyse or publish.

Oliver, D. G., Serovich, J. M., & Mason, T. L. (2005). Constraints and opportunities with interview transcription: Towards reflection in qualitative research. Social Forces, 84(2), 1273–1289.
Brislin, R. W. (1970). Back-translation for cross-cultural research. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 1(3), 185–216.

erhebung-1.problem: Key figures and statements sit scattered across long PDFs and reports; copying them into a spreadsheet by hand is slow and invites transcription errors and inconsistent definitions.
erhebung-1.result: A table built on a predefined extraction form, each value with page number and verbatim quote as provenance, 'not reported' where absent, and an error rate from your own verification sample.
steps: Define the unit of analysis and each field's operational definition
Pilot the form on one document and refine definitions
Ask for page numbers, quotes and 'not reported' markers
Verify a random sample and record the error rate

concepts: Data extraction form

A predefined list of fields with operational definitions, units and allowed values, piloted on a few documents before full use. Standard in systematic reviews across fields; it keeps extraction consistent across documents, people and tools.
Double extraction and verification

Two people extract independently and resolve discrepancies, or one extracts and a second verifies. With AI as first extractor, verify every value you will analyse, or at least a random sample with a recorded error rate.
Provenance: page and verbatim quote

Recording where each value comes from makes extraction auditable and exposes invented values quickly. Distinguish 'not reported' from 'zero' and from 'unclear', and never let the extractor estimate a missing value.
Document analysis (Bowen)

A systematic procedure for reviewing printed and electronic documents – skimming, thorough reading, interpretation – with attention to authenticity, credibility, representativeness and the purpose for which each document was produced.

refs.cite: Higgins, J. P. T., Thomas, J., Chandler, J., Cumpston, M., Li, T., Page, M. J., & Welch, V. A. (Eds.). (2019). Cochrane handbook for systematic reviews of interventions (2nd ed.). Wiley.
Bowen, G. A. (2009). Document analysis as a qualitative research method. Qualitative Research Journal, 9(2), 27–40.

practice.task: You extract the same fields from four attribution studies into one table. You learn how often Copilot quotes correctly, cites the right page and reports likelihood changes and return periods accurately – or mixes them up across papers.
practice.prompt: Attached are four attribution studies: Christidis et al. (2020) on UK 40 °C, Christidis et al. (2023) on 50 °C in the Mediterranean and Middle East, Zachariah et al. (2023) on the India–Pakistan heatwave and Schumacher et al. (2024) on the 2022 European drought. Extract into one table, one row per paper: event or extreme; region; variable and threshold; observational data used; climate models used; counterfactual (for example pre-industrial or natural-only world); headline result for likelihood or return period; headline result for intensity. For every value give the page number and a short verbatim quote. Write 'not reported' if a paper does not state a field; do not estimate, and do not use sources outside the PDFs. Then offer the table as a CSV file.

erhebung-2.problem: Coding hundreds of texts by hand takes weeks, and a second coder for reliability is often unavailable – so large text collections stay unused or are sampled thinly.
erhebung-2.result: A pre-coded table with quoted reasons and confidence, plus Cohen's kappa and a confusion matrix against your own codes – showing where the codebook is unclear before you trust the model at scale.
steps: Write a codebook with definitions, inclusion and exclusion rules
Code a sample yourself before asking Copilot
Ask for codes, quoted reasons and confidence per text
Compute Cohen's kappa and a confusion matrix in Python
Revise definitions where disagreements cluster; re-test on new texts

concepts: Codebook (content analysis)
Each code has a name, a definition, inclusion and exclusion criteria, and typical and borderline examples. Clear exclusion rules matter most for language models, which otherwise stretch codes to fit.
Cohen's kappa

Agreement between two coders corrected for chance: κ = (pₒ – pₑ) ÷ (1 – pₑ). By the Landis and Koch (1977) convention, 0.41–0.60 is moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial and above 0.80 almost perfect; these labels are conventions, not tests.
Krippendorff's alpha

Reliability coefficient that handles more than two coders, missing codes and nominal to ratio data. Krippendorff suggests α ≥ 0.80 for firm conclusions and ≥ 0.667 for tentative ones – again a convention.
Confusion matrix and sample size

Cross-tabulating your codes against the model's shows which code pairs get confused. Kappa from small samples is unstable and depends on code prevalence; report the number of texts and test on texts not used to refine the codebook.

refs.cite: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.
Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.
Krippendorff, K. (2018). Content analysis: An introduction to its methodology (4th ed.). Sage.

practice.task: You code the 12 practice abstracts by study type, then let Copilot code them with the same scheme and compute kappa. You learn how codebook clarity drives agreement, and how unstable kappa is with only 12 texts.
practice.prompt: I am testing whether a language model can pre-annotate texts. Attached are the 12 practice papers on climate change; read only each paper's abstract. Coding scheme, one code per paper: DATASET – describes how an observational data record is built or updated; ATTRIBUTION – quantifies the human contribution to warming or to a specific extreme; TREND – quantifies observed or projected changes without formal attribution; METHOD – mainly demonstrates a statistical technique on existing data. Use 'unclear' if no code fits; do not create new codes. Return a table: first author and year, code, confidence (high, medium or low), and a one-sentence reason quoting the abstract. Next I will paste my own codes: then compute Cohen's kappa in Python, show a confusion matrix and list every disagreement.
practice.check: Recompute kappa by hand from the confusion matrix. Expect disagreement on borderline papers such as Forster et al. (2025) and Vautard et al. (2023), and confirm that each quoted reason appears verbatim in the abstract.

tech.text: Upload the texts as a CSV with your codebook to Copilot Chat; Copilot codes them and computes Cohen's kappa in Python against your codes. Coding at scale needs a scripted pipeline in an approved tool. Practise on the 12 practice abstracts.

erhebung-3.problem: Fixed questionnaires cannot follow up vague or surprising answers, while live interviews do not scale – so you trade depth against reach, and AI follow-ups risk leading respondents.
erhebung-3.result: A piloted interview flow with every follow-up and its reason logged, so you can judge where the AI leads, presses or drifts – before ethics review and before any real respondent sees it.
steps: Set core questions and explicit rules for neutral probes
Answer as an invented respondent, including vague replies
Classify each logged follow-up as neutral or leading
Flag pressing or off-topic questions and tighten the rules
Obtain ethics approval and disclose the AI interviewer

concepts: Neutral probing

Follow-ups that ask for clarification or elaboration without suggesting an answer, such as 'Could you tell me more?' or 'What do you mean by …?'. Leading probes ('Wasn't that frustrating?') introduce interviewer bias; log each probe to audit it.
Standardised versus conversational interviewing

Standardised interviewing reads items verbatim and allows only neutral probes; conversational interviewing lets the interviewer clarify meaning. Schober and Conrad (1997) found clarification improved accuracy for complicated cases but lengthened interviews – AI follow-ups inherit this trade-off.
Interviewer effects and social desirability

Respondents adjust answers to the perceived interviewer and give socially desirable responses on sensitive topics. An AI interviewer changes these effects but does not remove them; pilot sensitive wording with particular care.
Informed consent for AI-mediated data collection

Participants must know they are talking to an AI, what happens to their answers (storage, processing location, third parties) and that they can stop at any time. This needs ethics approval and an approved platform, not Copilot Chat.

refs.cite: Schober, M. F., & Conrad, F. G. (1997). Does conversational interviewing reduce survey measurement error? Public Opinion Quarterly, 61(4), 576–602.
Fowler, F. J., & Mangione, T. W. (1990). Standardized survey interviewing: Minimizing interviewer-related error. Sage.
Groves, R. M., Fowler, F. J., Couper, M. P., Lepkowski, J. M., Singer, E., & Tourangeau, R. (2009). Survey methodology (2nd ed.). Wiley.

erhebung-4.problem: Suitable secondary data often exist but sit across statistics offices, archives and repositories you do not know – you find them after collecting your own, or overlook licence and definition differences.
erhebung-4.result: A shortlist of verified datasets with coverage, unit of analysis, access conditions, licence and gaps against your variables – a quicker route to data, or a clear case for collecting your own.

Ask Copilot for candidate datasets in a table
Open each link; confirm variables, licence and version
Read the documentation to judge fitness for your purpose
Drop unverifiable entries and rank the rest by fit

concepts: Fitness for use (Wang & Strong)

Data quality is judged relative to your purpose in four categories: intrinsic (accuracy, provenance), contextual (relevance, coverage, timeliness, granularity), representational (format, documentation) and accessibility (licence, access route). Assess each against your question.
FAIR principles

A quick screen for reuse: is the dataset Findable (persistent identifier such as a DOI), Accessible (clear access route), Interoperable (standard format) and Reusable (licence, provenance, documentation)? Without a licence you cannot assume reuse rights.
Datasheets and documentation

Good datasets document motivation, composition, collection process, preprocessing, intended uses, distribution and maintenance (Gebru et al. 2021). Read this documentation, codebook or user guide before trusting any summary Copilot gives.
Constraints of secondary data

Reused data were collected for another purpose: variables may be defined differently, reference periods and units may differ, and versions change. Record the version and access date of every file you use.
