erhebung-5.problem: Pseudonymising transcripts by hand is tedious, and indirect identifiers – a rare job title, a local event – are easy to miss, so combinations can still re-identify participants.
erhebung-5.result: A pseudonymised draft, a replacement log and the share of planted direct and indirect identifiers it missed – evidence of what your manual check must still catch before analysis.
steps: Write an invented excerpt with planted direct and indirect identifiers
List every planted identifier by type
Ask for replacements, flags and a replacement log
Compute recall: the share of planted identifiers caught
Keep the full manual check and use only approved environments

concepts: Pseudonymisation versus anonymisation (UK GDPR)

Pseudonymised data replace identifiers but can be re-linked with a separately kept key, so they remain personal data. Anonymous data can no longer reasonably identify anyone. Most qualitative transcripts are pseudonymised, not anonymous.
Direct and indirect identifiers

Direct identifiers name a person (name, email, address). Indirect or quasi-identifiers – job title, employer, rare event, age, place – identify in combination. Sweeney (2002) formalised protection as k-anonymity: every combination should match at least k people.
Recall and precision of de-identification

Recall is the share of real identifiers the tool caught; precision is the share of its replacements that were real identifiers. For confidentiality recall matters most, since one miss can re-identify, so measure it on planted identifiers.
Consistent replacement and analytic integrity

Use one stable pseudonym per person and category labels such as [CITY] or [ORG1], and store the replacement log separately and securely. Over-redaction can destroy analytic meaning; record what you changed and why.

refs.cite: Sweeney, L. (2002). k-anonymity: A model for protecting privacy. International Journal of Uncertainty, Fuzziness and Knowledge-Based Systems, 10(5), 557–570.
Saunders, B., Kitzinger, J., & Kitzinger, C. (2015). Anonymising interview data: Challenges and compromise in practice. Qualitative Research, 15(5), 616–632.

tech.text: Paste invented text into Copilot Chat to test detection only. Real transcripts go only into an environment your institution has approved for personal data, every output is checked by hand, and the AI step is declared in your methods.

erhebung-6.problem: Old print and handwriting slow you down: deciphering one page in an unfamiliar hand can take an hour, before translation even begins.
erhebung-6.result: A line-by-line diplomatic transcription with uncertain readings marked, an error count from your spot-check, and a literal translation of confirmed lines – a faster start to close reading, still verified against the image.
steps: Upload one page; state language, script and period
Ask for a diplomatic transcription with uncertainty marks
Count errors in five lines against an existing transcription
Translate only the lines you have confirmed

concepts: OCR and HTR

Optical character recognition reads printed text; handwritten text recognition reads manuscripts and usually needs models trained on similar hands. General chat models are not trained on your hand and may produce fluent but invented readings.
Diplomatic versus normalised transcription

Diplomatic transcription keeps original spelling, abbreviations, punctuation and line breaks; normalised transcription modernises them for readability. Decide before transcribing and state the convention, because normalising is already interpretation.
Character error rate (CER)

Standard accuracy measure for OCR and HTR: (substitutions + deletions + insertions) ÷ characters in a ground-truth transcription. Measure it yourself on a sample; fluent output with a high error rate is the main risk.
Source criticism

Assess the document's authenticity, provenance, date and purpose before interpreting it, and treat any machine translation as a draft, since the historical meaning of words may differ from modern usage.

analyse-0.problem: You know which model you need but lose hours on syntax, error messages and package options, and forum code rarely matches your data structure or the model's assumptions.
analyse-0.result: Commented, runnable code you can explain line by line, with the model's assumptions listed and tested, and one key estimate reproduced in a second tool.
steps: Name the model, software, outcome and predictors
Ask for commented code with assumption checks built in
Run it and paste error messages back verbatim
Reproduce one key estimate in a second tool

concepts: Ordinary least squares (OLS) assumptions

Linear regression gives unbiased, efficient estimates if the model is linear in its parameters and errors have mean zero, constant variance (homoscedasticity) and no autocorrelation; normal residuals matter for small-sample inference. Check each with residual plots and tests.
Heteroscedasticity-consistent (robust) standard errors

White's (1980) estimator, with small-sample variants such as HC3 (heteroscedasticity-consistent type 3), corrects standard errors when residual variance is not constant. Use it for cross-sectional data; it changes standard errors and p-values, not the coefficients.
Newey–West (HAC) standard errors

Heteroscedasticity- and autocorrelation-consistent standard errors for time series, where successive residuals are correlated (Newey & West, 1987). You choose a lag length; report it as part of the method.
Reproducible analysis script

One script that loads the raw data, records every transformation and prints the results, with software and package versions noted (Sandve et al., 2013). You, a supervisor or an examiner can rerun it exactly.

refs.cite: White, H. (1980). A heteroskedasticity-consistent covariance matrix estimator and a direct test for heteroskedasticity. Econometrica, 48(4), 817–838.
Newey, W. K., & West, K. D. (1987). A simple, positive semi-definite, heteroskedasticity and autocorrelation consistent covariance matrix. Econometrica, 55(3), 703–708.
Sandve, G. K., Nekrutenko, A., Taylor, J., & Hovig, E. (2013). Ten simple rules for reproducible computational research. PLoS Computational Biology, 9(10), e1003285.

analyse-1.problem: Raw files arrive with missing-value codes, quality flags, provisional rows and duplicates; cleaning by hand is slow, undocumented and hard to reproduce or defend later.
analyse-1.result: A rerunnable cleaning script, a log of every decision and a tidy dataset in which missing values, flags and exclusions are explicit rather than silently dropped.
steps: Upload the raw file and describe its source
Ask for a problem profile before changing anything
Decide each fix yourself and record why
Compare row counts and two values before and after

concepts: Tidy data

Wickham's (2014) structure: each variable a column, each observation a row, each type of observational unit a table. Much cleaning means reshaping messy layouts – wide year-by-month tables, header lines, units rows – into this form.
Missing-data mechanisms (MCAR, MAR, MNAR)

Rubin's (1976) classification: missing completely at random, missing at random given observed variables, or missing not at random. The mechanism decides whether deleting cases, imputing or modelling the missingness is defensible.
Screen, diagnose, edit

Van den Broeck et al.'s (2005) cycle: screen for anomalies, diagnose each as error, true extreme or undetermined, then correct, keep or flag it – documenting every decision. Do not delete values only because they are extreme.
Tukey's fences
A convention for flagging candidate outliers: values below Q1 − 1.5 × IQR or above Q3 + 1.5 × IQR, where IQR is the interquartile range. A flag is a prompt for diagnosis, not a rule for removal.

refs.cite: Wickham, H. (2014). Tidy data. Journal of Statistical Software, 59(10), 1–23.
Rubin, D. B. (1976). Inference and missing data. Biometrika, 63(3), 581–592.
Van den Broeck, J., Cunningham, S. A., Eeckels, R., & Herbst, K. (2005). Data cleaning: Detecting, diagnosing, and editing data abnormalities. PLoS Medicine, 2(10), e267.

analyse-2.problem: First-pass coding takes weeks, and alone it is hard to tell whether codes are applied consistently, whether themes are more than topic summaries, or when new data stop adding codes.
analyse-2.result: A draft coding frame with definitions and verbatim evidence that you test against your own reading – a sparring partner for coding that leaves interpretation and theme development with you.
steps: Practise on published or invented texts, never participant data
Ask for codes with definitions and verbatim quotes
Check that every quote exists and fits its code
Record where your reading differs and why

concepts: Braun & Clarke reflexive thematic analysis

Six phases: familiarisation, coding, generating themes, reviewing, defining and naming, writing up. Themes are patterns of shared meaning the researcher constructs, not topic summaries; as subjectivity is treated as a resource, AI output can only prompt your reflection.
Grounded theory coding

Developed by Glaser and Strauss and later Charmaz: initial (open) coding close to the data, focused coding of the most significant codes, then theoretical coding, linked by constant comparison and memo-writing. Use it when building theory from data.
Codes and themes; first- and second-cycle coding

A code labels a feature of a data segment; a theme is a broader pattern of meaning around a central concept. Saldaña distinguishes first-cycle methods (e.g. descriptive, in vivo) from second-cycle methods (e.g. pattern coding).
Saturation

The point at which new data add no new codes. Guest et al. (2006) found most codes in their interview study within the first twelve interviews – an empirical result for a fairly homogeneous sample, not a universal sample-size rule.

refs.cite: Braun, V., & Clarke, V. (2006). Using thematic analysis in psychology. Qualitative Research in Psychology, 3(2), 77–101.
Guest, G., Bunce, A., & Johnson, L. (2006). How many interviews are enough? An experiment with data saturation and variability. Field Methods, 18(1), 59–82.
Saldaña, J. (2021). The coding manual for qualitative researchers (4th ed.). SAGE.

analyse-3.problem: Hundreds of open-text answers, abstracts or documents are too many to read closely, and labelling them by hand is slow and hard to keep consistent across time and coders.

Upload the texts with an ID column
Hand-code a sample and compare with Copilot's labels
Rerun with other settings and compare stability

concepts: Validate, validate, validate

Grimmer and Stewart's (2013) principle: automated text methods are neither right nor wrong in general, so every application must be checked against human judgement on your own material before you report results.
Precision, recall and F1

Measures against a hand-coded gold standard: precision is the share of texts given a label that truly belong to it, recall the share of true cases that were found, F1 their harmonic mean. Report them per category.
Latent Dirichlet allocation (LDA)

A probabilistic topic model treating each document as a mixture of topics and each topic as a distribution over words (Blei et al., 2003). Results depend on the number of topics, preprocessing and random seed, and need many documents.
Zero-shot classification with large language models

Labelling texts from category definitions in a prompt, without training examples. Gilardi et al. (2023) found it outperformed crowd workers on several annotation tasks, but performance varies by task and model and must be checked on your data.

refs.cite: Grimmer, J., & Stewart, B. M. (2013). Text as data: The promise and pitfalls of automatic content analysis methods for political texts. Political Analysis, 21(3), 267–297.
Blei, D. M., Ng, A. Y., & Jordan, M. I. (2003). Latent Dirichlet allocation. Journal of Machine Learning Research, 3, 993–1022.
Gilardi, F., Alizadeh, M., & Kubli, M. (2023). ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks. Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, 120(30), e2305016120.

analyse-4.problem: Before formal analysis you need to know what a dataset contains, but coding every quick question slows you down, and exploratory patterns easily turn into untested claims.
analyse-4.result: A documented first look at structure, distributions and patterns, with the code behind every number, labelled as exploratory and kept apart from the hypotheses you will test.
steps: Upload the file and state source, unit and period
Ask one plain-language question at a time
Request the code behind every reported number
Record patterns as questions, not findings
Verify one result in your own software

concepts: Exploratory data analysis (EDA)
Tukey's (1977) approach of examining data with summaries and graphics to discover structure, anomalies and questions before modelling. It generates hypotheses; it does not test them.
Anscombe's quartet

Four datasets with near-identical means, variances, correlations and regression lines but very different scatterplots (Anscombe, 1973). It shows why you plot data rather than trust summary statistics alone.
Exploratory versus confirmatory analysis

Patterns found while exploring cannot be confirmed with the same data. Presenting them as if predicted is HARKing – hypothesising after the results are known (Kerr, 1998). Label exploratory results and test them on new data or a preregistered analysis.
Reference period (baseline)

Anomalies and indices are expressed relative to a reference period or category. Series with different baselines are comparable only after re-expressing them on a common one, which shifts their levels but not their trends.

refs.cite: Tukey, J. W. (1977). Exploratory data analysis. Addison-Wesley.
Anscombe, F. J. (1973). Graphs in statistical analysis. The American Statistician, 27(1), 17–21.
Kerr, N. L. (1998). HARKing: Hypothesizing after the results are known. Personality and Social Psychology Review, 2(3), 196–217.

analyse-5.problem: Default charts rarely meet journal guidelines, often hide uncertainty or use misleading colour scales, and adjusting every figure by hand for each revision is slow and unrepeatable.
analyse-5.result: A publication-ready figure produced by code you keep, with an encoding and palette chosen for accurate perception, so a revision means rerunning a script rather than redrawing.
steps: State the figure's single message and audience
Choose the encoding that makes the key comparison easiest
Show uncertainty and use a colour-blind-safe palette
Set size, fonts and resolution to journal rules
Save the code next to your data

concepts: Cleveland & McGill's perceptual ranking

People judge position on a common scale most accurately, followed by length, angle and slope, area, and finally colour and shading. Encode the comparison that matters most as position; avoid pie charts and 3D effects for precise comparisons.
Data-ink ratio
Tufte's principle that most of the ink in a graphic should show data: remove heavy gridlines, frames, shadows and redundant labels, while keeping axes, units and uncertainty.
Perceptually uniform, colour-vision-deficiency-safe palettes

Colour maps such as viridis or Crameri's scientific colour maps change lightness evenly and stay readable with colour-vision deficiency (Crameri et al., 2020); rainbow ('jet') maps create false boundaries and should be avoided.
Showing uncertainty

Plot intervals – confidence or credible bands, error bars – together with the estimate, and state in the caption what they represent (for example a 95 % confidence interval) so readers do not over-read small differences.

refs.cite: Cleveland, W. S., & McGill, R. (1984). Graphical perception: Theory, experimentation, and application to the development of graphical methods. Journal of the American Statistical Association, 79(387), 531–554.
Rougier, N. P., Droettboom, M., & Bourne, P. E. (2014). Ten simple rules for better figures. PLoS Computational Biology, 10(9), e1003833.
Crameri, F., Shephard, G. E., & Heron, P. J. (2020). The misuse of colour in science communication. Nature Communications, 11, 5444.

analyse-6.problem: Research code grows without tests or documentation; months later you cannot tell whether a change altered a result, and others cannot run, reuse or cite your code.
analyse-6.result: Explained, refactored code with docstrings and unit tests that pin down its behaviour, including edge cases – fewer silent errors and software you can deposit and cite.

Check the explanation matches your intent
Ask for unit tests, including edge cases
Run the tests before accepting any refactoring
Add a licence, README and citation file before sharing

concepts: Unit and regression tests

Unit tests check that a small function returns the expected output for given inputs, including edge cases such as empty, missing or extreme values; regression tests check that results do not change after refactoring. Tools: pytest, testthat.
Good enough practices in scientific computing

Wilson et al. (2017): decompose code into functions, eliminate duplication, use meaningful names, make dependencies explicit, provide a small test dataset, track changes with version control and deposit code in a DOI-issuing repository.
FAIR principles for research software (FAIR4RS)

FAIR adapted to code (Barker et al., 2022): software is findable through a persistent identifier and metadata, accessible, interoperable through standard formats and interfaces, and reusable through a licence, documentation and provenance.
Floating-point arithmetic

Computers store most decimals approximately, so results can differ in the last digits between machines or operation orders (Goldberg, 1991). Compare floats in tests with a tolerance, for example pytest.approx, never with exact equality.

refs.cite: Wilson, G., Bryan, J., Cranston, K., Kitzes, J., Nederbragt, L., & Teal, T. K. (2017). Good enough practices in scientific computing. PLoS Computational Biology, 13(6), e1005510.

Barker, M., Chue Hong, N. P., Katz, D. S., Lamprecht, A.-L., Martinez-Ortiz, C., Psomopoulos, F., Harrow, J., Castro, L. J., Gruenpeter, M., Martinez, P. A., & Honeyman, T. (2022). Introducing the FAIR Principles for research software. Scientific Data, 9, 622.
Goldberg, D. (1991). What every computer scientist should know about floating-point arithmetic. ACM Computing Surveys, 23(1), 5–48.

analyse-7.problem: Categories that seem clear in your head turn vague in use: coders disagree on borderline passages, rules scatter across memos, and agreement cannot be reported.
analyse-7.result: A codebook with definitions, inclusion, exclusion and borderline rules and anchor examples from your material, tested with a second coder and an agreement statistic you can report.
steps: Give your research question and four to six categories
Ask for definitions, inclusion, exclusion and borderline rules
Add anchor examples quoted from your own material
Code a sample independently with a second coder
Compute agreement, discuss disagreements and tighten the rules

concepts: Qualitative content analysis

A systematic, rule-guided method for categorising text (Mayring; Kuckartz & Rädiker). Categories are built deductively from theory or inductively from the material, and each is documented in a codebook with definition, coding rules and anchor examples.
Codebook entry

For each category: name, definition, inclusion criteria, exclusion criteria (often pointing to a neighbouring category), a rule for borderline cases and an anchor example – a typical passage quoted verbatim from your own material.
Cohen's kappa

Agreement between two coders corrected for chance: κ = (pₒ − pₑ) / (1 − pₑ) (Cohen, 1960). Landis and Koch's (1977) widely used but arbitrary convention: 0.41–0.60 moderate, 0.61–0.80 substantial, 0.81–1.00 almost perfect.
Krippendorff's alpha
A reliability coefficient for any number of coders, missing data and nominal to ratio scales. Krippendorff's convention: α ≥ 0.800 for reliable data; 0.667 to 0.800 only for tentative conclusions.

refs.cite: Cohen, J. (1960). A coefficient of agreement for nominal scales. Educational and Psychological Measurement, 20(1), 37–46.
Landis, J. R., & Koch, G. G. (1977). The measurement of observer agreement for categorical data. Biometrics, 33(1), 159–174.
Kuckartz, U., & Rädiker, S. (2023). Qualitative content analysis: Methods, practice and software (2nd ed.). SAGE.

analyse-8.problem: Statistical output is full of figures whose meaning and thresholds you half remember, and turning it into a correct, complete APA results paragraph takes repeated checking.
analyse-8.result: A plain explanation of your output, assumptions and quality criteria checked against sourced conventions, and a draft paragraph reporting effect sizes and intervals – usable once every number is verified.

Ask for each figure and the source of each threshold
Request an APA paragraph using only output numbers
Check every number and claim against the output

concepts: APA Journal Article Reporting Standards (JARS-Quant)

Appelbaum et al. (2018) list what quantitative results must report: sample size and missing data, each test with its statistic, degrees of freedom and exact p, effect sizes with confidence intervals, and any assumption violations.
p-values versus effect sizes

The American Statistical Association statement (Wasserstein & Lazar, 2016): a p-value measures neither the probability that a hypothesis is true nor the size of an effect, and p < .05 alone should not drive conclusions.
Model-fit cut-offs for structural equation models

Hu and Bentler's (1999) conventions: comparative fit index (CFI) ≥ 0.95, root mean square error of approximation (RMSEA) ≤ 0.06, standardised root mean square residual (SRMR) ≤ 0.08. Derived from simulations, they are guidelines, not pass–fail rules.
Heterotrait–monotrait ratio (HTMT)

A discriminant validity criterion, used especially in partial least squares structural equation modelling (Henseler et al., 2015). Conventional thresholds: below 0.85 for conceptually distinct constructs, below 0.90 for similar ones.
Reliability: Cronbach's alpha and McDonald's omega
Alpha assumes equal factor loadings (tau-equivalence); omega does not and is often preferred (McNeish, 2018). Values of about 0.70 or higher are a common convention for research use.

refs.cite: Appelbaum, M., Cooper, H., Kline, R. B., Mayo-Wilson, E., Nezu, A. M., & Rao, S. M. (2018). Journal article reporting standards for quantitative research in psychology: The APA Publications and Communications Board task force report. American Psychologist, 73(1), 3–25.
Wasserstein, R. L., & Lazar, N. A. (2016). The ASA statement on p-values: Context, process, and purpose. The American Statistician, 70(2), 129–133.
Hu, L., & Bentler, P. M. (1999). Cutoff criteria for fit indexes in covariance structure analysis: Conventional criteria versus new alternatives. Structural Equation Modeling, 6(1), 1–55.

querschnitt-0.problem: Supervision time is short: without an agenda key decisions slip, expectations stay implicit, and agreed actions sit in scattered notes that nobody writes up.
querschnitt-0.result: A timed agenda with the decisions you need and an action list with owners and deadlines checked against your notes – better-used meetings and a shared written record.
steps: Paste your progress notes and open questions
Ask for a timed agenda and three decisions
After the meeting, turn your notes into SMART actions
Check each action against your notes
Share the action list with your supervisors

concepts: Lee's approaches to doctoral supervision

Lee (2008) distinguishes five approaches: functional (project management), enculturation (joining the discipline), critical thinking, emancipation (personal development) and relationship development. Naming the approach an agenda item needs clarifies what you ask your supervisor for.
SMART actions

Doran's (1981) criteria for objectives: specific, measurable, assignable (now often 'achievable'), realistic and time-related. An action with a named owner and a deadline can be checked at the next meeting.
Decision and action log

A running record that separates decisions (what was agreed and why), actions (who does what by when) and open questions. It makes progress traceable for annual reviews and protects both you and your supervisors.

refs.cite: Lee, A. (2008). How are doctoral students supervised? Concepts of doctoral research supervision. Studies in Higher Education, 33(3), 267–281.
Doran, G. T. (1981). There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives. Management Review, 70(11), 35–36.

querschnitt-1.problem: Annual and transfer reviews arrive at busy times; reconstructing a year of progress from scattered notes and fitting it to the panel's criteria takes days.
querschnitt-1.result: A draft under your form's headings with gaps marked [TO ADD], a risk register and evidence of skills development – a starting point you complete with verified facts.

Add bullet notes and last year's objectives
Ask for a risk register with likelihood and impact
Map training to the Researcher Development Framework
Check every achievement and date against your records

concepts: Vitae Researcher Development Framework (RDF)

A UK framework of researcher competencies in four domains: knowledge and intellectual abilities; personal effectiveness; research governance and organisation; engagement, influence and impact. Use it to evidence training and skills development in reviews.
Risk register and likelihood–impact matrix

Each risk is listed with likelihood and impact (for example scored 1–5), their product as priority, a mitigation and an owner, following the logic of ISO 31000 risk management. Review it at each milestone.
SMART objectives
Doran's (1981) criteria: specific, measurable, assignable or achievable, realistic and time-related. Next year's objectives written this way can be assessed at the following review.

refs.cite: Vitae. (2010). Researcher development framework. Careers Research and Advisory Centre.
International Organization for Standardization. (2018). Risk management – Guidelines (ISO Standard No. 31000:2018).
Doran, G. T. (1981). There's a S.M.A.R.T. way to write management's goals and objectives. Management Review, 70(11), 35–36.

tech.text: Paste headings and notes into Copilot Chat, or upload last year's report as a Word file for continuity. Leave out health and personal circumstances; gaps appear as [TO ADD], not invented content.

querschnitt-2.problem: A doctorate is hard to plan backwards; people systematically underestimate how long tasks take, weeks fill with teaching and admin, and after a setback the plan feels obsolete.
querschnitt-2.result: A backward plan with milestones, dependencies and explicit buffers, a realistic week plan and a quick re-plan after setbacks – an honest view of whether your timeline holds.
steps: Give submission date, fixed milestones and weekly hours
Plan backwards and mark the critical path
Base estimates on past durations, then add buffers
Plan next week in half-day blocks
Re-plan after a setback and compare

concepts: Planning fallacy

The tendency to underestimate the time your own tasks will take, even when similar past tasks overran (Kahneman & Tversky, 1979; Buehler et al., 1994). Counter it by basing estimates on how long comparable tasks actually took.
Reference class forecasting

Estimating a task from the actual outcomes of a class of similar past tasks rather than from its own plan (Flyvbjerg, 2006). For a thesis: use how long your last chapter, ethics application or dataset really took.
Critical path method
Identifies the longest chain of dependent tasks; any delay on it delays submission, while tasks off it have slack. Protect the critical path with an explicit buffer before submission.
Backward planning
Start from the fixed end date and place milestones in reverse order, including lead times such as supervisor feedback and formatting, so you see the latest start date for each stage.

refs.cite: Buehler, R., Griffin, D., & Ross, M. (1994). Exploring the "planning fallacy": Why people underestimate their task completion times. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 67(3), 366–381.
Kahneman, D., & Tversky, A. (1979). Intuitive prediction: Biases and corrective procedures. TIMS Studies in Management Science, 12, 313–327.
Flyvbjerg, B. (2006). From Nobel Prize to project management: Getting risks right. Project Management Journal, 37(3), 5–15.

tech.text: Everything happens in Copilot Chat with pasted dates and commitments; ask for the plan as a table to copy into Excel, Planner or your calendar, and discuss it with your supervisor.

querschnitt-3.problem: Notes, highlights and annotations sit in different tools; you remember reading something relevant but cannot find it, and connections between sources stay in your head.
querschnitt-3.result: An overview of sources by concept, with key claims, methods, tags and typed links – supports, contradicts, extends – that structures your notes tool for later search and synthesis.
steps: Upload a handful of reading notes or abstracts
Ask for a concept matrix of claims and methods
Ask for typed links between sources, with evidence
Agree a small controlled tag vocabulary
Check two suggested links against the originals

concepts: Webster & Watson concept matrix
A table with sources as rows and concepts as columns that turns a review from author-centric to concept-centric (Webster & Watson, 2002). It shows which concepts are well covered and where gaps lie.
Zettelkasten (slip-box)

Luhmann's note system: atomic notes with one idea each, written in your own words, with a unique ID and explicit links to other notes. Links rather than folders create structure, so new connections become visible over time.
Controlled vocabulary
A fixed list of defined tags used consistently, as opposed to ad hoc tagging. Keeping 10–20 defined tags avoids synonyms such as 'heatwave', 'heat wave' and 'extreme heat' that split your searches.
Typed citation relations

Labelling why one source relates to another – supports, disputes, extends, uses method of – as formalised in the Citation Typing Ontology (CiTO; Peroni & Shotton, 2012). Typed links speed up synthesis more than plain 'related' tags.

refs.cite: Webster, J., & Watson, R. T. (2002). Analyzing the past to prepare for the future: Writing a literature review. MIS Quarterly, 26(2), xiii–xxiii.
Peroni, S., & Shotton, D. (2012). FaBiO and CiTO: Ontologies for describing bibliographic resources and citations. Journal of Web Semantics, 17, 33–43.

(2023). 1) Create a concept matrix with one row per paper and columns for research aim, data, method, main finding and three suggested tags. 2) List up to five links between the papers, each typed as supports, contradicts, extends or uses the method of, with a verbatim quote and page number from each paper as evidence. 3) Suggest a controlled vocabulary of 10–15 tags, each with a one-line definition, suitable for Zotero. querschnitt-4.problem: Data deposit and replication packages come last, when details are forgotten; codebooks and READMEs get rushed, flags go undocumented and numbers in the paper may not reproduce.
querschnitt-4.result: A codebook computed from the file, a README and repository metadata draft, and a replication checklist – data others can find and reuse, and results you can show are reproducible.
steps: Upload the dataset and describe how it was collected
Ask for a codebook computed from the file
Draft a README and DataCite metadata fields
Choose a licence and a repository that issues DOIs
Check two columns and every [CHECK] mark yourself

concepts: FAIR principles

Wilkinson et al. (2016): data should be findable (persistent identifier, rich metadata), accessible (retrievable by standard protocols), interoperable (shared vocabularies and formats) and reusable (clear licence, provenance, community standards). FAIR does not require data to be open.
DataCite Metadata Schema

The metadata standard behind most dataset DOIs. Mandatory properties are identifier, creator, title, publisher, publication year and resource type; recommended ones such as description, subject and rights make a record easier to find and reuse.
Codebook (data dictionary)

Documents each variable: name, label, type, unit, valid range or codes, missing-value codes and flags, and how it was derived. The Data Documentation Initiative (DDI) provides a standard for social and survey data.
Reproducibility and replicability

The National Academies (2019): reproducibility means consistent results from the same data, code and conditions; replicability means consistent results across studies that collect new data. A replication package secures reproducibility.

refs.cite: Wilkinson, M. D., Dumontier, M., Aalbersberg, I. J., Appleton, G., Axton, M., Baak, A., … Mons, B. (2016). The FAIR Guiding Principles for scientific data management and stewardship. Scientific Data, 3, 160018.
National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine. (2019). Reproducibility and replicability in science. The National Academies Press.

querschnitt-5.problem: At submission you must declare your AI use, but months later you cannot reconstruct which tool, prompt or output shaped which part of the thesis, or how you checked it.
querschnitt-5.result: A running provenance log of AI use, checks and the decisions they informed, plus a declaration drafted only from that log and aligned with your university's policy.

Record which research decision each use informed
Keep the log as a Copilot Page or in Excel

concepts: Disclosure of AI use (COPE)

The Committee on Publication Ethics (2023): AI tools cannot be authors because they cannot take responsibility; authors must state how and which tools were used, for example in the methods or acknowledgements, and remain accountable for all content.
Living guidelines on generative AI in research

European Commission (2024) guidance: researchers remain responsible for outputs, use AI transparently, protect privacy and confidentiality, respect intellectual property, and avoid substantial use in sensitive activities such as peer review or evaluating proposals.
Provenance record

Following the World Wide Web Consortium's PROV model, each entry links an entity (the output), the activity that produced it (prompt, date, tool and version) and the agent responsible (you), so any AI-influenced passage can be traced to its origin.
UK Concordat to Support Research Integrity
Names five elements of research integrity: honesty, rigour, transparency and open communication, care and respect, and accountability. A log of AI use is evidence of transparency and rigour.

European Commission, Directorate-General for Research and Innovation. (2024). Living guidelines on the responsible use of generative AI in research. Publications Office of the European Union.
Universities UK. (2019). The concordat to support research integrity. Universities UK.

querschnitt-6.problem: Courses rarely match your method or timing, documentation assumes knowledge you lack, and passively reading tutorials feels productive but leaves little you can apply.
querschnitt-6.result: A paced tutorial on your own example, built on worked examples and retrieval practice, with exercises and feedback – faster learning, provided you check functions against the official documentation.
steps: Name the skill and let Copilot test your level
Study one worked example, then solve a similar exercise
Answer before you ask for the solution
End with a quiz and repeat it days later
Check functions against the official documentation

concepts: Retrieval practice (testing effect)
Actively recalling information, for example in a quiz, improves long-term retention more than rereading (Roediger & Karpicke, 2006). Ask the tutor to test you before it explains again.
Worked-example effect

From cognitive load theory (Sweller, 1988): novices learn faster by studying fully worked solutions before solving similar problems; as expertise grows, worked steps are faded and you solve problems independently.
Spaced practice

Spreading practice over several days rather than massing it in one session improves retention. Dunlosky et al. (2013) rate practice testing and distributed practice as the most useful of ten common learning techniques.
Scaffolding and fading
Support is given at the start and gradually withdrawn. Ask the tutor for hints before full solutions, so that you do the thinking and it only fills gaps.

refs.cite: Roediger, H. L., III, & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.
Sweller, J. (1988). Cognitive load during problem solving: Effects on learning. Cognitive Science, 12(2), 257–285.

Dunlosky, J., Rawson, K. A., Marsh, E. J., Nathan, M. J., & Willingham, D. T. (2013). Improving students' learning with effective learning techniques: Promising directions from cognitive and educational psychology. Psychological Science in the Public Interest, 14(1), 4–58.

Then teach step by step in short chunks: explain one idea, show a small worked example, and give me one exercise; wait for my answer and give feedback before showing the solution. Use the attached HadCET monthly text file: help me read it, keep only complete years and use the Annual column (-99.9 marks missing values). Cover mean-shift versus trend-shift models and penalties such as BIC and MDL. Use the attached Shi et al. (2021) preprint as the reference and tell me which section each step relates to. querschnitt-7.problem: You repeat the same rules in every chat, and multi-step tasks such as a scoping search drift off course or mix unchecked, sometimes invented, sources into the output.
querschnitt-7.result: A reusable assistant that applies your citation style and terms, and a staged workflow that proceeds only after you have checked each stage – time saved while you stay accountable.
steps: Write standing rules and one narrow question
Create an agent with rules and trusted sources
Test it with one routine question first
Approve each stage only after checking every source
Log the workflow and declare the AI use

concepts: Human-in-the-loop checkpoints

The workflow stops after defined stages – search, extraction, synthesis – and continues only after a person has verified the output. Responsibility stays with you, and early errors do not propagate into later stages.
Automation bias

The tendency to over-trust automated output and miss its errors, stronger under time pressure and when a system is usually right (Parasuraman & Manzey, 2010). Checkpoints only help if you actually open and read each source.
Hallucination and grounding

Language models can produce fluent but unsupported or fabricated content (Ji et al., 2023). Grounding answers in supplied documents (retrieval-augmented generation) reduces but does not remove this risk; every citation still needs checking.
Arksey & O'Malley scoping review framework

Five stages: identify the research question, identify relevant studies, select studies, chart the data, and collate, summarise and report the results. An agent can assist with stages, but selection and charting decisions remain yours.

refs.cite: Arksey, H., & O'Malley, L. (2005). Scoping studies: Towards a methodological framework. International Journal of Social Research Methodology, 8(1), 19–32.
Parasuraman, R., & Manzey, D. H. (2010). Complacency and bias in human use of automation: An attentional integration. Human Factors, 52(3), 381–410.

Ji, Z., Lee, N., Frieske, R., Yu, T., Su, D., Xu, Y., Ishii, E., Bang, Y. J., Madotto, A., & Fung, P. (2023). Survey of hallucination in natural language generation. ACM Computing Surveys, 55(12), Article 248.

practice.task: Create an agent with four attribution PDFs as knowledge and run an extraction stage with a checkpoint. You learn how often extracted numbers, return periods and likelihood changes are wrong or unsupported, and why each stage needs your approval.
practice.prompt: You are the research assistant of a PhD researcher. Standing rules: cite in APA 7; 'return period' means the average time between events of a given size; 'probability ratio' means how many times more likely an event is with human influence; never invent sources, quotes or numbers, and say when you are unsure; use only the four attached PDFs (Christidis et al., 2020; Christidis et al., 2023; Zachariah et al., 2023; Schumacher et al., 2024). Work in two stages and stop after each for my approval. Stage 1, extraction: a table with one row per paper – event and region, variable, method, change in likelihood, change in intensity, future projection – each cell with a verbatim quote and page number. Stage 2, after my approval: a 200-word comparison citing only approved cells, ending with a list of claims I should still verify.

querschnitt-8.problem: Alerts and tables of contents bring dozens of new titles each week; skimming them all takes hours, and relevant papers are lost in the noise.
querschnitt-8.result: A weekly triage into must-read, maybe and skip against explicit relevance criteria, with reasons and suggested alert terms – less time sorting, a clear reading list and better-tuned alerts.
steps: Write your question and three relevance criteria
Paste the week's titles and abstracts
Ask for a rating and reason per paper
Spot-check skipped papers for relevant ones missed
Open the must-reads and make the final call

concepts: Relevance (eligibility) criteria

Explicit inclusion and exclusion rules – population or object, method, outcome, setting, date – as used in systematic screening. Writing them down makes triage consistent and lets you check why a paper received its rating.
Precision and recall in screening

Precision is the share of papers rated must-read that are truly relevant; recall is the share of truly relevant papers that were caught. When staying current, a missed key paper usually costs more than an extra abstract, so favour recall.
Forward and backward snowballing

Following the references of key papers (backward) and the papers that cite them (forward), as systematised by Wohlin (2014). Citation alerts on seed papers catch relevant work that keyword alerts miss.
Living review
A review that is continually updated as new evidence appears (Elliott et al., 2014). A weekly triage log is a personal, informal version that keeps your literature chapter current until submission.

refs.cite: Wohlin, C. (2014). Guidelines for snowballing in systematic literature studies and a replication in software engineering. In Proceedings of the 18th International Conference on Evaluation and Assessment in Software Engineering (Article 38). ACM.

Elliott, J. H., Turner, T., Clavisi, O., Thomas, J., Higgins, J. P. T., Mavergames, C., & Gruen, R. L. (2014). Living systematic reviews: An emerging opportunity to narrow the evidence-practice gap. PLoS Medicine, 11(2), e1001603.

Attached are twelve PDFs (in batches if needed); treat them as this week's alert. publikation-0.problem: You know your argument too well to see it from outside – a missing warrant, an unstated limitation or a section in the wrong place often only surfaces in peer review.
publikation-0.result: A three-sentence summary to test against your intent, a Toulmin map of claim, grounds, warrant and qualifiers with weak links marked, and a structure matched to the journal.
steps: Write a reverse outline: one sentence stating each section's point
Ask Copilot to map your argument as Toulmin elements
Check the introduction moves from territory to gap to aim
Fix the weakest warrant before polishing any wording
Check the structure against the journal's author guidelines

concepts: Toulmin model of argument

Breaks an argument into claim, grounds (evidence), warrant (why the evidence supports the claim), backing, qualifier (how strongly) and rebuttal (when it would not hold). Use it to find steps you assume but never state.
CARS model (Swales)

Create a Research Space: introductions typically make three moves – establish the territory, establish a niche (gap or problem), occupy the niche (aim, questions, contribution). Use it to test whether your introduction leads to your research question.
IMRaD

Introduction, Methods, Results and Discussion – the dominant structure for empirical articles across fields. Journals vary it (combined Results and Discussion, methods at the end), so the author guidelines decide.
Reverse outlining
Write one sentence per paragraph or section stating its point, then read only these sentences in order. Gaps, jumps and repetition become visible before you edit the prose.

refs.cite: Toulmin, S. E. (2003). The uses of argument (Updated ed.). Cambridge University Press.
Swales, J. M. (1990). Genre analysis: English in academic and research settings. Cambridge University Press.

Quote the sentence each element is based on. 3) Mark any step that is assumed rather than shown. 4) Identify the three CARS moves in the introduction – establishing the territory, establishing the niche, occupying the niche – quoting one sentence for each. Do not rewrite the text; refer to section headings and quote exactly.

publikation-1.problem: Writing in a second language takes longer, and generic editing tools smooth your text into phrasing that shifts hedges, emphasis or meaning and no longer sounds like you.
publikation-1.result: A clearer paragraph in given–new order and a change table you decide on line by line – terms, numbers, hedges and citations untouched, AI-typical phrases flagged for you to rewrite.
steps: Paste one paragraph and name your discipline and readers
Ask for edits by given–new order and plain-language principles
Check that no hedge, term, number or citation changed
Accept or reject each change; rewrite flagged phrases yourself
Check your university's proofreading rules before editing a thesis

concepts: Given–new principle (Gopen & Swan)

Readers expect familiar information at the start of a sentence (topic position) and the new, emphasised point at the end (stress position), with subject and verb close together. Use it to fix sentences that are correct but hard to follow.
Hedging

Calibrated qualification of claims (may, suggests, is likely to) that signals how strong the evidence is. Hyland shows it is a core feature of research writing; an edit that removes or adds a hedge changes your claim.
Plain-language principles

Prefer concrete verbs to nominalisations ('we analysed' rather than 'an analysis was carried out'), the active voice where the actor matters, one main idea per sentence and consistent terms. They improve clarity without simplifying content.
Authorial voice

The recognisable stance and phrasing that make a text yours. Formulaic phrases ('plays a crucial role', 'delve into') and empty intensifiers weaken it and are common in AI-generated text; rewrite them rather than accept them.

refs.cite: Gopen, G. D., & Swan, J. A. (1990). The science of scientific writing. American Scientist, 78(6), 550–558.
Hyland, K. (1998). Hedging in scientific research articles. John Benjamins.

practice.task: Edit the abstract of the Vautard et al. (2023) paper as if it were your own paragraph. You learn whether Copilot keeps hedges, uncertainty ranges and technical terms intact or quietly strengthens claims while improving the flow.
practice.prompt: Attached is the Vautard et al. (2023) PDF. Take its abstract (the paragraph before the introduction) and treat it as my own draft for a climate science journal. Edit it for clarity, precision and flow in UK English, applying the given–new principle: familiar information at the start of a sentence, the new point at the end. Keep the meaning, technical terms, numbers, uncertainty ranges and hedges (such as 'can be due to') unchanged, and add no content. Return 1) the edited abstract and 2) a table: original phrase, change, reason. Mark any sentence whose meaning is unclear instead of guessing, and flag generic or AI-typical phrasing.

publikation-2.problem: After many revisions, numbers in the abstract no longer match the tables, terms and abbreviations drift, and citations go missing from the reference list – reviewers notice.

Ask for a cross-check of numbers, terms and citations
Verify each flagged item in the document yourself

Use rule-based checks and your reference manager where they apply

concepts: Internal consistency audit

A systematic cross-check of every reported number, term and abbreviation across abstract, main text, tables and figures, and of in-text citations against the reference list in both directions. Run it after the last substantive revision.
GRIM test

Granularity-Related Inconsistency of Means: checks whether a reported mean is arithmetically possible given the sample size when data are integers, such as Likert items. An example of a rule-based check that is more reliable than reading.
statcheck

A tool that recomputes p-values from reported test statistics and degrees of freedom in APA format and flags inconsistencies. Nuijten et al. used it to show that such reporting errors are common in published psychology articles.
Error seeding

Planting known errors to estimate how many a checker finds (its detection rate or sensitivity), a technique from software testing. One planted mismatch tells you whether to trust Copilot's 'no issues found'.

publikation-3.problem: Finding a journal whose aims and scope fit, then reformatting references and layout to its guidelines, takes hours – and a desk rejection for poor fit costs weeks.
publikation-3.result: A shortlist of legitimate journals with links to their own guidelines, a formatting checklist for your choice, and references converted to its style with missing BibTeX fields flagged.

Confirm scope, article type and limits on the journals' own pages
Check unfamiliar journals with Think. Check. Submit. and DOAJ

concepts: Aims and scope fit

Editors desk-reject manuscripts outside a journal's stated aims and scope or article types. Judge fit from the aims and scope page, accepted article types and recent issues, not from the journal title.
Think. Check. Submit.

A cross-publisher checklist for judging whether a journal is trustworthy: known publisher and editorial board, transparent peer review and fees, indexing (for open-access journals, the Directory of Open Access Journals, DOAJ). Use it against predatory journals.
Citation style families

Author–date styles (APA 7, Harvard, Chicago author–date) cite name and year in the text and sort references alphabetically; numeric styles (Vancouver, IEEE, Nature) number citations by order of appearance. The journal's guide decides the details.
BibTeX entry types and fields

Each entry type has required fields: @article needs author, title, journal and year; @incollection (a chapter in an edited book) needs booktitle and publisher. Volume, pages and DOI are optional to BibTeX but expected by most journals.
CRediT taxonomy
Contributor Roles Taxonomy: 14 roles such as conceptualisation, methodology, formal analysis and writing – original draft. Many journals ask for a CRediT statement at submission.

refs.cite: Allen, L., Scott, J., Brand, A., Hlava, M., & Altman, M. (2014). Publishing: Credit where credit is due. Nature, 508(7496), 312–313.
American Psychological Association. (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association (7th ed.).

Give a table: journal, publisher, why it fits, article type and word limit, reference style, open-access options, link to the author guidelines page. Use only the journals' own websites and cite the link; if you are unsure of a detail, say so. 2) Convert references 1 to 5 of the PDF into BibTeX, choosing the correct entry type for each, and flag missing fields. publikation-4.problem: Critical feedback usually arrives months after submission, and supervisors rarely have time to read every draft as a sceptical outsider who checks methods, inference and reporting standards.
publikation-4.result: Three reviews from different angles, each tied to a quoted passage, missing reporting items named against the relevant EQUATOR guideline, and a prioritised revision roadmap – you judge which comments are valid.

Ask for methods, theory and devil's advocate reviews
Require a quoted passage behind every major comment
Check reporting items against the guideline's own checklist
Turn the comments you accept into a prioritised roadmap

concepts: EQUATOR Network reporting guidelines

A curated library of design-specific checklists: CONSORT (randomised trials), STROBE (observational studies), PRISMA 2020 (systematic reviews), COREQ and SRQR (qualitative research), ARRIVE (animal research). Developed in health research, used across fields wherever these designs occur.
Peer-review criteria

Editors usually ask reviewers to judge originality, validity of methods and inference, significance and clarity, and to separate major comments (affecting the conclusions) from minor ones (presentation, wording).
Devil's advocate (red teaming)

A reviewer role that argues deliberately against the central claim – alternative explanations, confounding, overgeneralisation, selective reporting – to expose weaknesses before external reviewers do.
TOP Guidelines

Transparency and Openness Promotion: eight standards journals adopt at different levels – citation, data, code and materials transparency, design and analysis reporting, preregistration of studies and of analysis plans, and replication. Use them to anticipate data and code requests.

publikation-5.problem: Reviewer reports mix major and minor points across several reviewers; drafting a complete, courteous point-by-point response is slow, and one overlooked comment can delay acceptance.
publikation-5.result: A numbered table of every comment with your planned action, and a draft point-by-point letter with gaps marked for you to fill – nothing claimed that you did not change.
steps: Paste all comments and ask for a numbered table
Classify each as major or minor and add your action
Ask for a point-by-point letter quoting each comment
Give reasons and evidence where you disagree
Check every table row appears in the letter

concepts: Point-by-point response

The standard format for revisions: quote each comment, answer it directly, and state the change with its location (page, line or section). Keep the reviewers' numbering so editors can trace every point.
Major and minor revisions

Major comments concern design, analysis, validity or conclusions and usually need new work or substantial rewriting; minor comments concern clarity, presentation or references. Address all, but plan effort by this distinction.
Reasoned disagreement

You may decline a request: thank the reviewer, give your reasons with evidence or citations, and if possible make a smaller change (for example a limitation sentence). The editor decides, so write for the editor.
Open peer review

Publishing reviewer reports and author replies alongside the article, as in Copernicus interactive discussions, eLife or F1000Research. Ross-Hellauer identifies traits such as open identities, open reports and open interaction; published reports are models for your own response.

refs.cite: Noble, W. S. (2017). Ten simple rules for writing a response to reviewers. PLOS Computational Biology, 13(10), e1005730.
Ross-Hellauer, T. (2017). What is open peer review? A systematic review. F1000Research, 6, 588.

publikation-6.problem: Chapters written over several years drift apart – a research question goes unanswered, findings repeat, and the golden thread from question to contribution that examiners look for gets lost.
publikation-6.result: A traceability matrix of each research question across chapters, with gaps, overlaps and repetition marked and quoted – a basis you check against the full chapters and discuss with your supervisor.
steps: Summarise each chapter yourself in three to five sentences
Ask for a research question by chapter traceability matrix
Have gaps and overlaps flagged with quotes from your summaries
Check the conclusion answers every question and states the contribution
Verify flagged issues in the full chapters yourself

concepts: Golden thread

The traceable line from the research problem and questions through literature, methodology and findings to conclusions and contribution. Examiners check that every question is posed, addressed and answered, and that nothing important appears from nowhere.
Doctorateness

Trafford and Leshem's set of interlinked features examiners look for – among them a stated gap, explicit research questions, a conceptual framework, appropriate methodology, conceptual conclusions and a contribution to knowledge – judged by how well they connect.
Traceability matrix

A table with research questions as rows and chapters (or sections) as columns, showing where each question is introduced, addressed, answered and discussed. Borrowed from requirements engineering; empty cells reveal gaps, repeated cells reveal overlap.
Thesis by publication

A thesis built from papers plus an integrative introduction and discussion. The linking chapters must show how separately published studies answer shared research questions and add up to one contribution.

refs.cite: Trafford, V., & Leshem, S. (2009). Doctorateness as a threshold concept. Innovations in Education and Teaching International, 46(3), 305–316.
Mullins, G., & Kiley, M. (2002). 'It's a PhD, not a Nobel Prize': How experienced examiners assess research theses. Studies in Higher Education, 27(4), 369–386.

practice.task: Treat the Christidis et al. (2020) and Christidis et al. (2023) papers as two chapters of a thesis by publication and test three given research questions against them. You learn whether Copilot detects a question that only one chapter answers.

Treat them as chapters 2 and 3 of a thesis by publication. The research questions are: RQ1 How has human influence changed the likelihood of extreme daily maximum temperatures at specific locations? RQ2 How will that likelihood change by 2100 under different emission pathways? RQ3 What do these changes imply for heat-related mortality? First summarise each chapter in five sentences. Then create a table, one row per research question, showing where each chapter introduces, addresses with methods, and answers it. List gaps, overlaps and repetition, quoting the sentence each point rests on. If the papers do not give enough information, say so.

publikation-7.problem: You rarely get to practise answering hard questions about your own thesis aloud before the viva, and mock vivas depend on busy colleagues' time.
publikation-7.result: A bank of likely examiner questions on originality, significance and rigour, each linked to your own claims, and practice answers with feedback – rehearsal alongside, not instead of, your supervisors.

Ask for questions on contribution, methodology, findings and future work
Answer one question at a time, ideally aloud
Ask for feedback and a probing follow-up per answer
Take the hardest questions to your supervisor

concepts: UK viva voce

An oral examination, usually with one internal and one external examiner, in which you defend the thesis against your university's doctoral criteria. Outcomes typically range from pass, minor or major corrections to resubmission; regulations differ by university.
FHEQ level 8 descriptors

The QAA's descriptors for doctorates: new knowledge created through original research of a quality to satisfy peer review, systematic command of a substantial body of knowledge, and the ability to conceive, design and carry out a research project.
Originality, significance, rigour
The criteria most examiners' questions return to: what is new, why it matters to the field, and whether methods and inference are sound. Practise one short answer for each about your own thesis.
Retrieval practice (testing effect)
Recalling and explaining material under questioning strengthens long-term retention more than rereading (Roediger & Karpicke 2006). Answering aloud also exposes points you cannot yet explain clearly.

refs.cite: Quality Assurance Agency for Higher Education. (2014). The frameworks for higher education qualifications of UK degree-awarding bodies. QAA.
Roediger, H. L., III, & Karpicke, J. D. (2006). Test-enhanced learning: Taking memory tests improves long-term retention. Psychological Science, 17(3), 249–255.

Imagine it is the core chapter of my PhD thesis and I face a viva at a UK university. Act as an experienced external examiner. Write 12 questions grouped under: contribution to knowledge, methodology, findings and limitations, and future work. Make some broad and some probing, and link each to a specific claim in the paper, quoting it. Then ask me one question at a time, wait for my answer, and give brief feedback on clarity, use of evidence and what an examiner might ask next.

publikation-8.problem: Wrong reference details and quotation errors – sources that do not say what they are cited for – slip in easily, especially with AI-suggested sources, and damage credibility.
publikation-8.result: A per-reference check against DOIs and publisher records, and a support rating (supports, partly supports, does not) for each citing sentence with quoted evidence – you open every flagged source and decide.

Ask for a DOI and metadata check per reference
Ask whether each source supports its sentence, quoting it
Open every flagged source and judge yourself

concepts: Quotation (citation) accuracy

Whether a cited source actually supports the statement it is cited for. Jergas and Baethge's meta-analysis found quotation errors common in medical journals, a substantial share of them major – the same check applies in every field.
Reference fabrication by language models

Language models can produce plausible but non-existent references or real ones with wrong details. Walters and Wilder found both problems in ChatGPT-generated bibliographies, so every AI-suggested reference needs an existence and metadata check.
DOI and Crossref metadata

A Digital Object Identifier resolves to the publisher's record; Crossref metadata confirm authors, year, title, journal, volume and pages. Resolving the DOI is the first existence check, comparing metadata the second.
Citation statement classification

scite classifies citing statements as supporting, contrasting or mentioning (Nicholson et al. 2021). Use the same logic for your rating: supports, partly supports, does not support – always with the quoted passage.

Walters, W. H., & Wilder, E. I. (2023). Fabrication and errors in the bibliographic citations generated by ChatGPT. Scientific Reports, 13, 14045.

Nicholson, J. M., Mordaunt, M., Lopez, P., Uppala, A., Rosati, D., Rodrigues, N. P., Grabitz, P., & Rife, S. C. (2021). scite: A smart citation index that displays the context of citations and classifies their intent using deep learning. Quantitative Science Studies, 2(3), 882–898.

publikation-9.problem: Turning a pile of notes into a first draft is slow, and on a blank page it is easy to lose track of which source supports which claim.
publikation-9.result: A claim–evidence map and a rough draft built only from your notes, with gaps marked – a starting point you verify sentence by sentence, rewrite in your own words and declare.

Ask for a claim–evidence map before any draft
Verify every sentence against your notes and sources
Rewrite the section in your own words
Declare the tool, purpose and your checks as required

concepts: Claim–evidence map

A table listing each planned claim with the source and page that supports it, built before drafting; empty cells mark gaps. It makes every sentence of the later draft traceable and is your main human check.
Concept matrix (Webster & Watson)
A grid of concepts against sources that turns an author-by-author summary into a concept-centric synthesis. Use it to order your points by argument rather than by paper.
Authorship and AI (COPE position)

AI tools cannot be listed as authors because they cannot take responsibility for the work. Authors must disclose how AI tools were used and remain fully accountable for the content, including any errors.
AI-use declaration
A short statement naming the tool, date, purpose and how you checked and changed the output, placed where your university or the journal requires (methods, acknowledgements or a declaration form).

refs.cite: Webster, J., & Watson, R. T. (2002). Analyzing the past to prepare for the future: Writing a literature review. MIS Quarterly, 26(2), xiii–xxiii.
Committee on Publication Ethics. (2023). Authorship and AI tools: COPE position statement. COPE.

- India–Pakistan heat, March–April 2022: about 1 °C hotter and 30 times more likely due to human-caused climate change (Zachariah et al., 2023).
- 2022 western–central European summer soil drought: about once in 20 years now, about once per century pre-industrially (Schumacher et al., 2024).
- Attribution results are increasingly used in adaptation planning.
First build an evidence map: points in order, each with its source, gaps marked. Then draft 200 words in APA style using only these notes, marking [GAP] wherever a sentence lacks a source. Add nothing of your own.

transfer-0.problem: Writing a lay summary, policy brief and social post for each paper takes time, and simplifying invites spin – causal, general or certain claims the paper does not make.

Ask for a lay summary and a policy brief outline
Derive a short social post from the summary
Check numbers, conditions and uncertainty terms against the paper

concepts: Plain-language summary

A short, jargon-free account of the question, approach, main finding and what it means, written for non-specialists. Keep the paper's uncertainty and conditions; explain one technical term rather than remove it.
Spin and exaggeration

Reporting that makes findings look stronger, more causal or more general than the study supports. Sumner et al. traced much exaggeration in health news to press releases; check claim strength, causal wording and generalisation.
Calibrated uncertainty language

The IPCC uses fixed likelihood terms – for example 'likely' for 66–100 % and 'very likely' for 90–100 % probability – plus confidence levels. A model for keeping uncertainty explicit when simplifying in any field.
Policy brief structure
One to two pages, conclusions first (inverted pyramid): the problem, key findings, implications and a few concrete, feasible recommendations, with a source for each finding.

transfer-1.problem: Turning results into a clear chart and talk takes many iterations, and slides often list topics instead of stating claims backed by visual evidence.

concepts: Assertion–evidence slide structure

Each slide headline is a full-sentence claim, and the body is visual evidence for it (chart, image, diagram) rather than a bullet list. Alley and colleagues report better audience comprehension than with topic-and-bullet slides.
Data-ink ratio
Tufte's principle: maximise the share of ink that shows data and remove decoration – heavy gridlines, 3D effects, redundant labels, 'chartjunk'.
Colour-vision-safe, perceptually uniform colour maps

Rainbow ('jet') colour maps distort data and exclude readers with colour-vision deficiency. Use perceptually uniform maps such as viridis or scientific colour maps (Crameri et al. 2020), and never encode meaning in colour alone.
Reproducible figures
Generate every chart by code from the data file and keep code and data together, so values can be checked and the figure regenerated after changes (Rougier et al. 2014).

transfer-2.problem: Bringing current research into seminars means building cases and questions from scratch, and recall questions are quicker to write than ones that make students apply or evaluate findings.
transfer-2.result: A seminar case, discussion questions at the apply level of Bloom's revised taxonomy or above, and a data exercise aligned to your learning outcome, with simplifications listed for you to check.
steps: Upload the paper with module, level and learning outcome
Ask for a 400-word case study based on the paper
Add questions and an exercise at apply level or higher
Check that outcome, activity and assessment align
Check case facts and figures against the paper

concepts: Constructive alignment

Biggs' principle that intended learning outcomes, teaching and learning activities, and assessment tasks are designed to match: students learn what the activity makes them do, so the activity must require what the outcome states.
Revised Bloom's taxonomy

Six cognitive process levels – remember, understand, apply, analyse, evaluate, create (Anderson & Krathwohl 2001). Write discussion questions and exercises at apply level or above when the outcome asks for more than recall.
Research–teaching nexus (Healey)

Four ways to bring research into teaching: research-led (learning findings), research-oriented (learning how research is done), research-tutored (discussing papers), research-based (students do inquiry). A data exercise moves a session towards research-based.
Case-based learning
Students work on a realistic, bounded scenario with a question or decision, applying concepts to evidence. Cases drawn from a real paper should keep its facts and say where they simplify.

refs.cite: Biggs, J. (1996). Enhancing teaching through constructive alignment. Higher Education, 32(3), 347–364.
Anderson, L. W., & Krathwohl, D. R. (Eds.). (2001). A taxonomy for learning, teaching, and assessing: A revision of Bloom's taxonomy of educational objectives. Longman.

Healey, M. (2005). Linking research and teaching: Exploring disciplinary spaces and the role of inquiry-based learning. In R. Barnett (Ed.), Reshaping the university: New relationships between research, scholarship and teaching (pp. 67–78). McGraw-Hill/Open University Press.

transfer-3.problem: Evidence that research reached policy, media or practice is scattered across the web, and mentions are easily mistaken for impact – a demonstrable change or benefit beyond academia.
transfer-3.result: A table of verified mentions with links, classified by type and by stage from awareness to use, plus a short impact narrative that claims contribution, not more than the evidence shows.
steps: Give title, DOI and authors of one paper
Ask for mentions in policy, media and practice
Open each link and keep only confirmed items
Classify each as awareness, use or change
Draft a narrative claiming contribution, not sole attribution

concepts: Research impact (REF definition)

In the UK Research Excellence Framework, impact is 'an effect on, change or benefit to the economy, society, culture, public policy or services, health, the environment or quality of life, beyond academia', assessed for reach and significance.
Reach and significance

Reach is the extent and diversity of the people or organisations affected; significance is how much the research enabled, enriched or changed policies, practices or understanding. A news mention shows reach, rarely significance.
Contribution analysis
Mayne's approach: set out the pathway from research to change, collect evidence for each link and consider other influences, then claim a credible contribution rather than sole attribution.
Altmetrics

Indicators of online attention – news, policy documents, social media, blogs – tracked by services such as Altmetric and Overton. Attention is a lead for finding impact evidence, not evidence of impact itself.

refs.cite: REF 2021. (2019). Panel criteria and working methods (REF 2019/02). Research Excellence Framework.
Mayne, J. (2012). Contribution analysis: Coming of age? Evaluation, 18(3), 270–280.

The increasing likelihood of temperatures above 30 to 40 °C in the United Kingdom. Nature Communications, 11, 3093. https://doi.org/10.1038/s41467-020-16834-0. Search the web for mentions since 2020 in policy documents, government or NGO reports, news media and practitioner websites. Give a table: source, type (policy, media, practice), date, link, what it says about the research, and stage (awareness, use in decision-making, change in policy or practice). Include only items whose page names the paper, its DOI or its authors. If you are not sure an item refers to this paper, say so; do not invent sources.

transfer-4.problem: Reaching audiences in other countries needs more than literal translation – technical terms, units, number formats and examples have to fit local usage and the field's terminology.
transfer-4.result: A localised translation with a term glossary and listed adaptations, checked by back-translation in a fresh chat and reviewed by a fluent reader, since back-translation misses unnatural style.
steps: Paste the summary and name language, country and audience
Ask for translation, glossary and a list of adaptations
Back-translate in a new chat without the original
Compare meaning sentence by sentence with your original
Ask a fluent reader to check terms and style

concepts: Back-translation

Translating the target text back into the source language independently – here in a fresh chat – and comparing meaning with the original (Brislin 1970). It detects omissions and shifts in meaning but not unnatural or unidiomatic style.
TRAPD team translation

Translation, Review, Adjudication, Pretesting and Documentation: parallel translations discussed by a team, a decision on each disputed term, a test with target readers and a record of choices. The standard in cross-cultural survey research; stronger than back-translation alone.
Localisation
Adapting a text beyond the words: units, decimal and date formats, examples, institutions and cultural references, so that it works for readers in the target country.
Terminology management
Fixing one agreed equivalent for each key term in a glossary and checking it against field-specific term bases, such as IATE (Interactive Terminology for Europe) for EU languages.

refs.cite: Brislin, R. W. (1970). Back-translation for cross-cultural research. Journal of Cross-Cultural Psychology, 1(3), 185–216.

practice.task: Translate the abstract of the Christidis et al. (2020) paper for a non-specialist audience, then back-translate it in a new chat. You learn whether Copilot keeps terms such as 'return time' consistent and whether back-translation reveals shifts in meaning.

Take its abstract and translate it into German for interested members of the public in Germany (replace German and Germany with a language someone in your group reads and a matching country). Use a clear, natural style. Keep technical terms consistent and give a short glossary with the translated term for each key concept, such as return time, human influence, attribution and greenhouse gas emissions. Adapt anything that would not make sense locally and list every adaptation. Keep all numbers and units exact, using local number formats. Mark any term where you are unsure of the usual translation in climate science.

design-6.problem: Conceptual and measurement models are redrawn by hand in slide or drawing tools; each new paper or changed construct means rework, and the diagram drifts away from the text and the item list.
design-6.result: An editable model kept as code (Mermaid or draw.io XML) next to a construct–indicator table – updated in minutes when the literature changes, and consistent across thesis, slides and survey.
steps: Write each construct with a one-line definition and its expected paths
Generate the diagram as Mermaid or draw.io XML and a construct–indicator table
Decide reflective or formative measurement for every construct
Store the code with your project and regenerate it when the evidence changes
Check every arrow against your theory and every item against its source

concepts: Conceptual model

Shows constructs and the hypothesised relationships between them (direct paths, mediators, moderators). Each arrow should correspond to a stated hypothesis or proposition and its theoretical argument.
Measurement model
Links each latent construct to its observed indicators (e.g. survey items). Path-diagram convention: latent constructs as ovals, indicators as rectangles, arrows for assumed directions (Kline, 2016).
Reflective vs formative measurement

Reflective: the construct causes its indicators, which should correlate and are interchangeable. Formative: indicators jointly form the construct and are not interchangeable. Misspecification biases estimates (Jarvis et al., 2003).
Construct–indicator mapping
A table linking each construct definition to its items and their source; the basis for content validity and the later CFA or PLS-SEM (MacKenzie et al., 2011).
Model as code and living updates
Keeping the diagram as text (Mermaid, draw.io XML) makes it versionable and quick to regenerate, in the spirit of living reviews that are updated as new evidence appears (Elliott et al., 2014).

refs.cite: Jarvis, C. B., MacKenzie, S. B., & Podsakoff, P. M. (2003). A critical review of construct indicators and measurement model misspecification in marketing and consumer research. Journal of Consumer Research, 30(2), 199–218.

MacKenzie, S. B., Podsakoff, P. M., & Podsakoff, N. P. (2011). Construct measurement and validation procedures in MIS and behavioral research: Integrating new and existing techniques. MIS Quarterly, 35(2), 293–334.
Kline, R. B. (2016). Principles and practice of structural equation modeling (4th ed.). Guilford Press.

erhebung-7.problem: Card sorts, item-sorting tasks and workshop boards produce rich data on paper; typing them up and counting placements by hand takes hours and introduces transcription errors.
erhebung-7.result: A transcribed, structured table of every card and its placement, with counts per category and flagged uncertain readings – analysis can start the same day, and the photo remains the audit trail.
steps: Plan the board so categories and cards are clearly separated
Photograph it straight on and remove identifying details
Let Copilot transcribe first, then map cards to categories
Count placements per item, e.g. for substantive validity
Verify card count and five transcriptions against the photo

concepts: Card sorting (open and closed)

Participants group cards into categories they create (open) or into predefined ones (closed). Used to explore mental models or to test whether categories work; analysed via placement frequencies and clusters (Spencer, 2009).
Item-sorting task

Respondents assign each survey item to the construct definition it fits. The proportion of substantive agreement (psa) and the substantive-validity coefficient (csv) flag items that are misread before a full pre-test (Anderson & Gerbing, 1991).
Visual and photo data
Photos of boards are research data: they need a capture protocol (angle, light, labelling), consent where people or handwriting can be identified, and secure storage (Pain, 2012).
Transcription before interpretation
Separate the literal record (what is on each card, where) from coding and clustering. This keeps the step checkable and makes AI misreadings visible.

refs.cite: Anderson, J. C., & Gerbing, D. W. (1991). Predicting the performance of measures in a confirmatory factor analysis with a pretest assessment of their substantive validities. Journal of Applied Psychology, 76(5), 732–740.
Pain, H. (2012). A literature review to evaluate the choice and use of visual methods. International Journal of Qualitative Methods, 11(4), 303–319.
Spencer, D. (2009). Card sorting: Designing usable categories. Rosenfeld Media.
