design-7.problem: Building realistic stimuli for each condition – a mock feed, vignettes, product pages – and wiring them into a survey with randomisation takes weeks, and small unintended differences between conditions confound the results.
design-7.result: Matched stimuli for every condition, a manipulation check and a complete study flow with variable names – faster to build, easier to keep conditions equivalent, and data that go straight into your analysis.
steps: Define the manipulated factor, its levels and everything held constant
Generate stimuli per condition and list every difference between them
Add a manipulation check and the full survey flow with variable names
Pilot realism and the manipulation with real people
Obtain ethics approval and prepare a debrief

concepts: Experimental manipulation and control
Conditions should differ only in the manipulated factor; every other difference is a confound. Random assignment balances participant characteristics across conditions in expectation.
Manipulation check

A measure of whether participants perceived the manipulation as intended. Useful in pilots; in the main study it can itself influence responses, so place and use it deliberately (Hauser et al., 2018).
Vignettes and mock environments

Systematically varied descriptions or simulated settings such as a social media feed, combining control with realism. Factorial vignette designs vary several factors at once (Atzmüller & Steiner, 2010).
Stimulus sampling
One stimulus per condition confounds the manipulation with that stimulus' quirks; several stimuli per condition support generalisation beyond the specific material (Wells & Windschitl, 1999).
Deception and debriefing
If stimuli mislead – fictional posts, fake ads – ethics guidance requires justification, minimal deception and a debrief; AI-generated material should be labelled as such in the study record.

refs.cite: Hauser, D. J., Ellsworth, P. C., & Gonzalez, R. (2018). Are manipulation checks necessary? Frontiers in Psychology, 9, 998.
Atzmüller, C., & Steiner, P. M. (2010). Experimental vignette studies in survey research. Methodology, 6(3), 128–138.
Wells, G. L., & Windschitl, P. D. (1999). Stimulus sampling and social psychological experimentation. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 25(9), 1115–1125.

practice.task: Build the two conditions of a framing experiment: a mock news feed on a heatwave with and without an attribution statement taken from the papers. You see whether Copilot keeps the conditions equivalent and the attribution claim faithful to the source.
practice.prompt: Attached are Christidis et al. (2020) on UK hot days and Zachariah et al. (2023) on the 2022 heatwave in India and Pakistan. I want to test whether an attribution statement changes how worried readers are about heatwaves. Create two versions of a mock social media news feed as one self-contained HTML page each: six posts from fictional accounts, one of them a post about a heatwave. Condition A: the heatwave post includes one attribution sentence taken faithfully from one of the papers, with its source. Condition B: the same post without that sentence, otherwise word for word identical. erhebung-8.problem: Language models are tempting as cheap, instant 'respondents', but their answers do not represent real people; used naively, they produce data that look plausible yet are invalid for claims about humans.
erhebung-8.result: A defensible design for research where model outputs are the object of study – audits of accuracy, bias or consistency – with documented prompts, versions and variability, and clear limits on what can be concluded.
steps: Frame the question about the model, not about a human population
Fix prompts, model, version, date and parameters before collecting
Sample repeated answers and code them against a reference
Report variability and limitations; disclose the method
Use real participants for any claim about people

concepts: Silicon sampling and algorithmic fidelity

Conditioning a model on persona descriptions to simulate survey answers. Fidelity to human response patterns varies by topic and group and must be tested against real data, not assumed (Argyle et al., 2023).
Limits of synthetic respondents

Model answers can be unstable across prompts and versions, show too little variance and flatten or misportray identity groups; they cannot replace human samples for inference (Bisbee et al., 2024; Wang et al., 2025).
Model audits
Systematic, repeated querying of one or more models with fixed prompts to measure accuracy, bias or consistency – here the model is the unit of analysis.
Reproducibility and disclosure
Record model name and version, date, full prompts, settings such as temperature and the number of runs; publish prompts and raw outputs so others can repeat the study.

refs.cite: Argyle, L. P., Busby, E. C., Fulda, N., Gubler, J. R., Rytting, C., & Wingate, D. (2023). Out of one, many: Using language models to simulate human samples. Political Analysis, 31(3), 337–351.
Bisbee, J., Clinton, J. D., Dorff, C., Kenkel, B., & Larson, J. M. (2024). Synthetic replacements for human survey data? The perils of large language models. Political Analysis, 32(4), 401–416.

Wang, A., Morgenstern, J., & Dickerson, J. P. (2025). Large language models that replace human participants can harmfully misportray and flatten identity groups. Nature Machine Intelligence, 7(3), 400–411.

practice.prompt: In about 120 words, and with sources: how has human-caused climate change changed the likelihood of days above 40 °C in the UK, according to research published before the July 2022 record? [Run this exact prompt in five new chats and save every answer with the time.]
